docs.title: seqforge
docs.text: seqforge works out what a sequencing dataset actually is — which technology, which file holds what — and compiles that into a pipeline that processes it correctly. Your own sequencer, a core facility, a collaborator, a public archive: it does not matter where the files came from, or whether they sit on your disk or behind a URL (it can read what it needs from a remote FASTQ without downloading it).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Sequencing files do not say what they are.

To process a dataset you need what no FASTQ states: the technology, which file holds the barcodes, how long they are and where they start, which file holds the RNA, which direction it was read in.

What you have instead is prose — a sentence in a paper, a line in a spreadsheet, a README, an email, or nothing. The filenames are no help: _1 and _2 say nothing about which read is which.

So somebody guesses and types it into a config. When the guess is wrong, nothing crashes. The aligner exits successfully and hands you a count matrix that is quietly, unrecoverably wrong.

The answers are in the bytes. seqforge reads them, treats prose as a hypothesis to check, and stops when it cannot be sure.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["FASTQ files"] --> P["probe<br/><i>read the bytes</i>"]
    M["prose & metadata<br/><i>paper, README, database</i>"] --> H["harvest<br/><i>read the words</i>"]
    P --> R["resolve<br/><i>score & decide</i>"]
    H --> R
    KB[("knowledge base<br/>one entry per<br/>technology")] --> R
    R --> D["<span style='color:#fff'><b>dataset manifest</b><br/>what the data IS</span>"]
    D --> C["compose"]
    RECIPE["<span style='color:#fff'><b>processing manifest</b><br/>what to DO with it</span>"] --> C
    C --> OUT["<span style='color:#fff'>pipeline config<br/>+ module selection</span>"]

    %% colour lands on the wrapping element and loses to it — the text renders dark-on-dark.

The model proposes; code decides. Its job is prose: find claims and point at where it found each one. Every claim carries the sentence it came from, and code checks that the sentence really says that, or throws the claim away. The model never supplies a value of its own, never overrides the bytes, and nothing it produces reaches a manifest without passing a validator.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Dataset manifest — what the data is. Written once, identified by a hash of its contents.
  • Processing manifest — what to do with it: genome, aligner, introns or not. Many per dataset.

Run the same dataset three ways: three pipelines, one unchanged dataset manifest.

docs.title: When it doesn't know, it says so
docs.text:
A missing barcode file, metadata contradicting the bytes, two technologies indistinguishable where the choice would change the output — it stops, with a reason and a suggested fix. It does not emit the best-scoring guess. A guess is how the quiet failures happen.

Next: Getting started — or browse the technologies seqforge recognises.

docs.title: The easiest way: ask Claude
docs.text:
You don't have to run seqforge yourself. It ships a set of skills for Claude Code, so you can describe your data in plain words and let Claude drive the compiler — figuring out the technology, which file is which, and how to turn it into a runnable pipeline.

git clone https://github.com/liuhlab/seqforge
cd seqforge
pixi install
pixi run install-skills      # teach Claude how to drive seqforge

Then open Claude Code in the folder with your data and just say what you have:

Compile the single-cell RNA-seq data in ./data with seqforge. It's accession PRJNA1027859, and the paper is ./info/paper.pdf. Align against the ce11 genome, annotation WS298.

Claude hands you back a manifest (what your data is) and a Snakefile (the pipeline that processes it). You don't need to know the chemistry, which file holds the barcodes, or what any flag means — that's exactly what seqforge recovers from the files themselves. The full walkthrough, including what to do when Claude stops and asks a question, is in Compiling with Claude.

One thing worth knowing up front: reading a paper or sample sheet uses a language model, through the lab's model gateway. Open a tunnel to it and set LABLLM_GATEWAY to its local address (Reach the lab gateway says how); you need no provider key. If you have no prose to read, you can skip that and stay fully offline.

docs.title: Running it yourself
docs.text:
If you'd rather drive it directly — or you're batching thousands of datasets in a script — seqforge is a plain command-line tool. Every command prints JSON and reports what happened through its exit code. There is no --json flag; JSON is simply what comes out.

# 1. what do the bytes say?
pixi run -- seqforge probe reads/*.fastq.gz

# 2. which technology is this, and how confident are we?
pixi run -- seqforge resolve score reads/*.fastq.gz

# 3. (optional) what does the archive DECLARE about it?
pixi run -- seqforge io records PRJNA1027859

# 4. write down what the data IS  (immutable, content-addressed)
#    --accession fetches the records and joins them to your files, so each file
#    lands in its archive sample. Without one you still get a manifest -- samples
#    grouped by run. Most data has no accession.
pixi run -- seqforge manifest fill reads/*.fastq.gz --accession PRJNA1027859
pixi run -- seqforge manifest validate seqforge/manifest.yaml

# 5. write down what you want DONE with it  (one of many)
pixi run -- seqforge processing new seqforge/manifest.yaml \
    --assembly ce11 --annotation WS298 --out seqforge/processing.yaml

# 6. compile the two into something runnable
pixi run -- seqforge compose seqforge/manifest.yaml --processing seqforge/processing.yaml

Steps 4 and 5 are separate on purpose — see The two artifacts.

Artifacts land under seqforge/ in the working directory — visibly, because they are the point. manifest fill writes seqforge/manifest.yaml only once it validates clean; if it doesn't, you get seqforge/manifest.draft.yaml instead, and exactly one of the two exists.

For the whole thing on a real dataset, one command at a time with real output, see the step-by-step tutorial.

The data doesn't have to be local

seqforge can fingerprint a FASTQ straight from a URL without ever downloading it — seqforge io probe-remote <url> reads a small bounded slice over HTTP and identifies the library from that. Everything about identifying the data works the same whether the bytes are on your disk or on a remote server.

docs.title: Exit codes are the API
docs.text:
code meaning what to do 0 fine carry on 1 an error it broke; read the message 2 you used it wrong check the arguments 3 blocked the data can't be processed as-is. The blocker names a remedy 4 needs a human a real ambiguity. Answer it and re-run

3 and 4 are the point of the tool, not an inconvenience. See When it refuses.

Next: Compiling with Claude, or browse the supported assays.

docs.title: Files from the hand work
docs.text:
This page lists every file that the hand work on the standard set produced. It is written for someone outside the project who builds an evaluation on these files. For each kind of file it gives the path, the count, the format, who or which model made the file and how, and a few lines of Python that load it.

This page uses five words:

  • A study is one piece of research: the experiments one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet.
  • A Series is one deposit in GEO, the Gene Expression Omnibus, a public archive of sequencing data. A Series has an id such as GSE241718. One study can span several Series.
  • A study's bounds say which Series and which papers belong to the study.
  • The standard set is a fixed list of 50 small GEO studies.
  • A study's reading says what each sequenced sample is and which labels the study varied.

Hand work means work done one study at a time, outside the unattended chain that the study workflow describes. The name does not mean that a person did it. A model made every file on this page, or code wrote the file from a model's answer. No person has checked any of them.

docs.title: Every file in one table
docs.text:
All files are under evals/standard-set/ in the seqforge repository. <ID> is the Series that a study was picked by, and it is also the name of the study's folder. The counts were measured on 2026-11-19.

File Path Count Made by Format The pick pick.yaml 1 A model session, 2026-11-19 On this page The study file <ID>/study.yaml 50 The judge command On this page The bounds <ID>/bounds.yaml 50 Code, from the two models' answers The bounds file The job's bounds <ID>/job-bounds.yaml 50 The bounding job, typesafe/jev-1.14.0, 2026-11-21 The bounds file The draft <ID>/draft.yaml 50 deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash On this page The verdict <ID>/verdict.yaml 50 claude-fable-5-2 On this page The reading <ID>/reading.yaml 5 claude-fable-5-2 The reading file The reading's verdict <ID>/reading.verdict.yaml 5 claude-fable-5-2, in a second pass On this page The reading's notes <ID>/reading.notes.md 5 The model that wrote the reading Markdown text A person's answers none yet 0 Nobody yet The rule

That is 266 files: the pick, five files for each of the 50 studies, and three more for each of the five studies that have a reading. The folder also holds a README.md, which describes the commands.

This snippet counts the files again. Run it, and every other snippet on this page, from the root of the repository. Each snippet needs Python 3 and PyYAML and nothing else.

import collections
import pathlib

root = pathlib.Path("evals/standard-set")
print(len([p for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()]))  # 50
print(sorted(collections.Counter(p.name for p in root.glob("*/*")).items()))

The files hold identifiers and the models' own words. The only text of a record or of a paper in them is short quotes, most of them under passages in a reading. The records are public at GEO, and PubMed lists each paper by its number.

docs.title: The standard set
docs.text:
The 50 studies were picked on 2026-11-19. A small model then drafted each study's bounds, and a large model judged each draft once. Three commands did that work, and all three are now retired: a pass of the standard-set-bounds kind asked the small model about each study, the standard-set draft command wrote draft.yaml from the answers, and the standard-set judge command asked the large model about one study and wrote verdict.yaml, bounds.yaml and study.yaml. The bounding job now draws a study: the study workflow says how. You can load every file here without liulab-data, the lab's package that stores the GEO records and the papers.

The judge agreed with 48 drafts and replaced 2, those of GSE101112 and GSE126954. It was unsure about none.

docs.title: pick.yaml: the 50 picked, the spares and the replaced
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/pick.yaml. One file.

Made by: a model session on 2026-11-19. The file names no model. Its header says that the picker judged each study's direction, shape and design from the Series' public GEO record and the PubMed abstract of its paper. The picker read 302 Series records and 263 abstracts, a count taken from the note on record links.

The file has six top-level fields:

Field Holds store_build The build of liulab-data's store that the counts and the links were read from: 20261107T163933Z. picked_on The date of the pick: 2026-11-19. limits The size limits a study had to fit: the most samples, experiments and linked Series. The hard_shape_ limits are wider and apply to a study picked for a hard shape. studies The 50 picked studies: 17 on aging, 17 on neurodegeneration and 16 on C. elegans. spares 14 studies held back to take the place of a picked study that fails. replaced The studies taken out after the pick, each with the spare that took its place and the reason it failed. The list is empty: no study has been replaced.

Each entry of studies and of spares has these fields:

Field Holds id The Series the study was picked by. direction aging, neurodegeneration or c_elegans. A study counts under one. also_fits The other directions the study could count under. May be empty. hard_shape The hard case the study was picked for: recites_older_series, paper_over_several_series, superseries, series_with_two_studies or series_without_paper. null for a plain study. 34 of the 50 are null. linked_series Every Series linked to the picked one, the picked one included. pmids Every paper linked to any of those Series, each a PubMed number written as text. assay The kind of sequencing, in the picker's short words. compiles_today The library chemistry that the record's protocol text points to, by the name seqforge gives it. A list when the study has two, and null when seqforge supports none. No sequencing read was looked at. compiles_fully true when every library of the study is in a chemistry that compiles_today names. known_dataset true for a study that seqforge had already worked on before the pick. 5 of the 50. n_samples, n_experiments The GEO samples and the SRA experiments of all the linked Series together. design The design, in the picker's short words. reason_picked One or two sentences. status settled, shape_to_confirm or shape_not_found. The last one marks a study picked as possibly two studies in one Series that turned out to be one study. 3 of the 50. spare_for Spares only. The direction or the hard shape that the spare stands in for. 
import yaml

with open("evals/standard-set/pick.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    pick = yaml.safe_load(handle)
print(len(pick["studies"]), len(pick["spares"]), len(pick["replaced"]))  # 50 14 0
print(pick["studies"][0]["id"], pick["studies"][0]["reason_picked"])

docs.title: study.yaml: the facts about one pick
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/study.yaml. 50 files.

Made by: the retired standard-set judge command, when it wrote the verdict. It copies the pick's facts, takes summary from the draft, and adds three fields from the verdict. Each file was rewritten once, on 2026-11-20 (UTC), to move the bounds out into bounds.yaml.

Field Holds id The folder name: the Series the study was picked by. summary One short line that says what the study is. From the draft. direction, also_fits, hard_shape, reason_picked As in pick.yaml. store_build The store build the identifiers were read from. All 50 files say 20261107T163933Z-subset. The subset is a small copy of the build that pick.yaml names, cut down to the records of these studies. records Every linked record, by identifier only: series, superseries (which of those Series is a SuperSeries, or null), bioprojects and pmids. bounds_from draft when the judge agreed with the draft (48 files), judge when the judge's bounds replaced it (2 files). status settled, or unsure when the judge was unsure. All 50 say settled. read_to_decide What the judge had to read: records, abstract, full_paper. 
import yaml

with open("evals/standard-set/GSE241718/study.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    study = yaml.safe_load(handle)
print(study["id"], study["direction"], study["records"]["series"], study["bounds_from"])

docs.title: bounds.yaml: the study's bounds
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/bounds.yaml. 50 files.

Format: The bounds file describes every field. All 50 files say format: 1.

Made by: code, which converted the bounds that the two models drew. models.bounds names the model whose bounds became the study's: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash in 48 files and claude-fable-5-2 in 2. The files hold no date. Git history dates the conversion to 2026-11-20 (UTC).

The 50 files hold 74 claims: 57 Series kept and 17 records left out, in 10 studies. Seven studies have two Series. Four studies have no paper. In three studies the folder's Series is a SuperSeries, so it is in left_out and not in series: GSE117724, GSE140511 and GSE240375.

import pathlib

import yaml

for path in sorted(pathlib.Path("evals/standard-set").glob("*/bounds.yaml")):
    bounds = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    kept = [claim["id"] for claim in bounds["series"]]
    left_out = [claim["id"] for claim in bounds["left_out"]]
    print(bounds["study"], kept, bounds["papers"], left_out)

docs.title: draft.yaml: what the small model answered
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/draft.yaml. 50 files.

Made by: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, through the drafting pass and the draft command. The model read the records of the linked Series and the abstract of each paper, and nothing else. The drafts are dated from 2026-11-19 23:38 to 2026-11-20 00:05 (UTC).

Field Holds id The study. model The model that answered. pass The pass that asked: its kind, its version and its number, such as standard-set-bounds/2026.11.3/pass-5. The 50 drafts come from four passes. when The time of the answer, as text: 2026-11-20T00:02:16Z. summary One line that says what the study is. bounds The model's answer. See below. checks_failed What the code found malformed in the answer. Empty in 49 drafts. The draft of GSE126954 put a sample id among the left-out records.

bounds in a draft is the model's answer. It is not in the bounds format:

Field Holds series The Series the model kept. papers The papers the model kept, each written pmid:<number>. reason One line. left_out A mapping from each record left out to the reason. In bounds.yaml the same thing is a list of claims. split_samples An older field. See What this page promises. 
import yaml

with open("evals/standard-set/GSE241718/draft.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    draft = yaml.safe_load(handle)
print(draft["model"], draft["pass"], draft["when"])
print(draft["bounds"]["series"], draft["bounds"]["papers"], draft["bounds"]["left_out"])

docs.title: verdict.yaml: what the judge answered
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/verdict.yaml. 50 files.

Made by: claude-fable-5-2, through the judge command, once for each study. The judge got the draft and what the drafting model saw, and it could open the full records and the full text of the papers. The verdicts are dated from 2026-11-19 23:38 to 2026-11-20 00:10 (UTC).

Field Holds id The study. model The model that judged. when The time of the verdict, as text. agrees true when the judge agrees with the draft's bounds. 48 are true and 2 are false. bounds null when the judge agrees. Otherwise the judge's own bounds, with the same five fields as the bounds in a draft. reason Why the judge agrees or disagrees. unsure true when the judge could not decide. All 50 are false. read What the judge read: records, abstract, full_paper. The judge opened a full paper for 7 studies.

The bounds that the two models settled on are the draft's when the judge agrees, and the judge's when it does not:

import pathlib

import yaml

for folder in sorted(pathlib.Path("evals/standard-set").glob("GSE*")):
    draft = yaml.safe_load((folder / "draft.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    verdict = yaml.safe_load((folder / "verdict.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    answer = draft["bounds"] if verdict["agrees"] else verdict["bounds"]
    print(verdict["id"], verdict["agrees"], answer["series"], sorted(answer["left_out"]))

docs.title: The five worked readings
docs.text:
Five of the 50 studies have a reading, one for each kind of design. A model wrote each reading. A second model pass checked each reading against the records and the paper. No person has checked any of them. Where the second pass disagrees with a reading, the reading is left as written, and the disagreement is in the verdict.

Study Kind of design Samples Passages Second pass agrees Disagreements GSE100021 Two groups: a treatment against a control 8 29 No 1 GSE112068 A dose series and a time series 23 45 No 3 GSE235532 Pull-down libraries with their input controls 24 30 Yes 1 GSE117724 Two assays: 18 RNA-Seq libraries and 2 ChIP-Seq libraries 20 54 Yes 0 GSE241718 One paper over two Series 8 28 Yes 2

No command made these files. The process was:

  1. A large model read the records of the study's Series and its paper, and wrote reading.yaml and reading.notes.md. For four studies it read the records, the abstract and the full text. GSE112068 has no paper, so the model read the records only.
  2. A second pass read the same sources again and checked the reading. It looked for every quote in the field or the paper section that the reading names, and it compared the samples with the study's bounds. It wrote reading.verdict.yaml.
  3. The second pass changed a reading only to make it pass the format check. Each such change is listed under format_fixes in the verdict: 7 changes over the five readings.

Each file records the model as claude-fable-5-2, for the reading, for its probabilities and for the second pass.

docs.title: reading.yaml: the study reading
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.yaml. 5 files.

Format: The reading file describes every field. All five files say format: 2. They were written in format 1 and rewritten to format 2 on 2026-11-21. That change added the assay's ontology id, the source of the ids, and the passages that speak against a claim. No claim's text, number, level or p changed. Each reading.notes.md ends with what changed in it.

Made by: claude-fable-5-2, named in models.reading and in models.probabilities. The files hold no date. They were added to the repository on 2026-11-20 (UTC).

A sample has every claim under shared, except a label that its own row writes. The snippet applies that rule:

import yaml

with open("evals/standard-set/GSE241718/reading.yaml", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    reading = yaml.safe_load(handle)
for sample, row in reading["samples"].items():
    claims = {**reading["shared"], **row}  # a row's claim replaces the shared claim whole
    print(sample, claims["tissue"]["text"], claims["age"]["level"], claims["assay"]["p"])
print(reading["passages"][14]["quote"])  # a passage number loads as a whole number

The relations between the samples are not stored. seqforge study relations <file> derives them, and the reading file describes its output.

docs.title: reading.verdict.yaml: what the second pass found
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.verdict.yaml. 5 files.

Made by: claude-fable-5-2, in a second pass. The verdicts are dated from 2026-11-20 01:39 to 02:05 (UTC).

Field Holds id The study. model The model of the second pass. when The time of the verdict. Four files write it as text. GSE100021/reading.verdict.yaml writes it without quotes, so PyYAML returns a datetime for that one file. read What the second pass read: records, abstract, full_text. format_fixes A list of text. Each item is one change that the second pass made to reading.yaml so that the file passes the format check. quotes Three counts of the quotes in the reading: checked, found, and not_found, a list. In all five, every quote was found: 186 quotes together. samples_match_bounds true when the samples of the reading are exactly the samples of the Series in the study's bounds. true in all five. agrees The second pass's overall judgement of the reading. true in 3 and false in 2. A verdict can agree and still list disagreements. disagreements A list, one item for each point where the second pass would write the reading differently. May be empty. unsure A list of text: what the second pass could not settle from the sources. Each verdict has 3 to 6. reason The second pass's account of what it checked and found.

Each item of disagreements has five fields:

Field Holds where The place in reading.yaml, such as shared.dose or samples.GSM7720368.donor. One item can name several places. says What the reading says there. should_be What the second pass would write. why The reason. passages The passages that the point rests on, by number. One item in the verdict of GSE241718 also quotes a record line as text. 
import pathlib

import yaml

for path in sorted(pathlib.Path("evals/standard-set").glob("*/reading.verdict.yaml")):
    verdict = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(verdict["id"], verdict["agrees"], verdict["quotes"]["found"], len(verdict["unsure"]))
    for item in verdict["disagreements"]:
        print("  ", item["where"], "->", item["should_be"])

docs.title: reading.notes.md: what the format could not hold
docs.text:
Path: evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.notes.md. 5 files.

Made by: the model that wrote the reading, at the same time. Each file is free Markdown text with no fixed fields. It says what the model read and what the reading format could not hold for this study, or held badly.

import pathlib

for path in sorted(pathlib.Path("evals/standard-set").glob("*/reading.notes.md")):
    notes = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    print(path.parent.name, notes.splitlines()[0])

docs.title: Answers a person gave while checking
docs.text:
There are none yet. No person has answered a question about any of the 50 studies, and no person has corrected a file. Every study folder holds only the files in the table at the top.

The rule for the first one is fixed. An answer that a person gives while checking is saved as a small plain file. The file holds the question, the study, the answer, who gave it and when. No folder and no command exist for such files yet. When the first answer is saved, this page lists its path.

docs.title: What this page promises
docs.text:
Every file listed here is at the listed path, in the current format. There is one format at a time. A change to a format rewrites every existing file in the same change, and this page changes with it. The page does not promise that the content of a file stays the same.

Two kinds of file have a written format and a check:

seqforge study check-bounds evals/standard-set/<ID>/bounds.yaml
seqforge study check-reading evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.yaml

All 50 bounds files pass their check (measured on 2026-11-19), and all five readings pass theirs (measured on 2026-11-21).

The other files have no format number, and their fields are the ones this page lists. The drafts and the verdicts are kept as the models wrote them, so they hold fields from before the bounds format:

  • split_samples is in the bounds of all 50 drafts, and in the bounds of the 2 verdicts that have bounds of their own. It comes from when one Series could be split between two studies. A study is now whole Series, and the bounds format rejects the field. It is empty in all 50 drafts and in the verdict of GSE101112. In the verdict of GSE126954 it lists seven sample ids.
  • left_out in a draft or a verdict is a mapping from a record to a reason. In bounds.yaml it is a list of claims.
  • A paper is written pmid:<number> in the bounds, the drafts, the verdicts and the readings. In pick.yaml and in study.yaml it is the bare number, as text.
  • A full paper is full_paper in study.yaml and verdict.yaml, and full_text in the two reading files.

docs.title: Known wrong or stale facts in the files
docs.text:
Do not build on these lines without reading this list.

  1. GSE241718/study.yaml describes the two Series wrongly. Its reason_picked says that one Series holds whole cells and one holds nuclei. The protocol on every sample record, the summary of both Series and the paper say that all eight libraries are single-nucleus. The paper says that the data were uploaded in two stages. The entry in pick.yaml has the same sentence, and its assay and design say the same. That entry also names the chemistry as 10x-3p-gex, while the protocol on every sample record names a Singleron kit.
  2. GSE126954/bounds.yaml still speaks of seven samples. Its claim and its reason say that "the seven embryo samples are its own data". The judge had drawn the study as seven of the eight samples. A study is whole Series, so the bounds are now the whole Series of eight. The eighth sample is a re-deposited sample of an older study. Telling it apart is left to the study's reading, and this study has none yet.
  3. The bounds carry no probability and no quote. All 74 claims in the 50 bounds files are marked inferred, with the model's reason as the text. Every p is null, models.probabilities is null, and passages is empty. null means that no model has given a probability, not that the claim is in doubt.
  4. One when is later than its file. GSE100021/reading.verdict.yaml says 2026-11-20T02:05:00Z. The commit that added the file is dated 23 minutes earlier. The model wrote the time itself.
  5. The readings keep what the second pass disagrees with. The table below has one line for each reading.
Reading What the second pass disagrees with GSE100021 shared.dose writes the value 1.7e+12 with the unit viral_particles_per_side. The source sentence gives the content of the suspension, not the amount each side received. GSE112068 shared.sex is na and should be unknown, on all 23 samples. The three untreated samples have control as their treatment, where na fits. The time factor cites passages that do not list its levels. GSE117724 Nothing. The second pass lists four points it could not settle, such as the stage of the worms at harvest. GSE235532 The reading leaves out the time of collection, and its notes say wrongly that the format has no place for it. GSE241718 The donor ids of the four young libraries are a guess, and their p of 0.5 is too high. Passage 19 names two sample records, and all eight hold the quote.

The second pass also could not settle the age of the four aged libraries of GSE241718. The sample records say 24 months, and the Series designs and the paper say 26. The reading writes 26 with a p of 0.55.

docs.title: Passes and reviews
docs.text:
Some of seqforge's work asks a language model the same kind of question many times: once for each GEO Series, about 200,000 of them. seqforge runs that work as passes. A pass runs one unit kind over a list of units, each named by a key, and records how each unit ended. The engine behind it is the lab package liulab-llms. It sends every call through the lab gateway, caches every answer, stops at a dollar ceiling, and keeps the record in a task folder. seqforge names its kinds and starts their passes. The engine's words are defined in liulab-llms's glossary.

seqforge has one kind so far, study-bounds, which draws each study's bounds. The study workflow says how it is used.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need two things:

  • A tunnel to the lab gateway, and LABLLM_GATEWAY set to its local address, such as http://127.0.0.1:8000. Reach the lab gateway shows how to open one.
  • A local clone of the lab's review repo. Give it as --reviews DIR, or set SEQFORGE_REVIEWS to it. A pass reads the reviews in its reviews/ folder to learn which units a person has already answered. Make the clone with gh repo clone liuhlab/seqforge-review.

The review commands also need the GitHub CLI, gh, version 2.48 or later, logged in with gh auth login. They act on GitHub as you, and need no more than the repo scope that login gives by default.

docs.title: Start a pass
docs.text:
seqforge pass start <kind> --ceiling-usd 5

This runs the kind over its default units, in the kind's own order. Each unit ends in one of five ways:

Ending What it means settled The answer passed every check unsettled The answer failed a check, and a person or a stronger model should look refused The kind's code declined to answer the unit unfinished The pass stopped, or the unit's code failed, before it ended held An input the unit needs is missing

The options:

Option What it does --ceiling-usd The most the pass may spend, in dollars. Required: it has no default --model ROLE=PROVIDER/NAME[,KEY=VALUE...] The model for one role, such as writer=deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash,thinking=off. Repeat it for more roles. The keys are thinking (on or off), effort, temperature and max-output-tokens. A role you do not name takes the kind's default model --keys FILE Run exactly these units, one key per line, in this order --only ENDINGS Run only the units whose current ending is one of these, such as unsettled,refused --units-at-once How many units run at once. Default 32 --off-peak-only Send calls only outside the model's peak hours --label The pass's name in the gateway's record. Default: the kind's name --task DIR The task folder. Default: seqforge/passes/<kind>/ in the current folder --reviews DIR The review repo's clone, if SEQFORGE_REVIEWS does not name it

The gateway has no model aliases, so PROVIDER/NAME is the provider's exact model name. A --model value is the whole model: a setting you leave out takes liulab-llms's default, not the kind's.

docs.title: What it prints
docs.text:
While the pass runs, a progress line goes to stderr at most every 30 seconds. It gives the units ended so far, by ending, and the dollars spent. stdout carries one JSON object and nothing else:

Field Value kind, kind_version The kind, and its hand-set version task The task folder pass_id, label The pass's number in the task, and its label store_build The liulab-data store build the pass read, or null for a kind that reads no store models Each role's full model value keys How many units the pass was given counts How many units ended each way: settled, unsettled, refused, unfinished and held, zeros included stopped, message Why the pass stopped, and the gateway's message about it; both null when it reached its end spent_usd, first_cost_usd What the pass spent, and what its answers cost when each was first paid, answers from the cache included requests, cache_hits Requests sent to providers, and answers that came from the cache

A kind that reads liulab-data's store opens it once, when the pass starts. The whole pass reads that one build, even if the store is refreshed while it runs.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Exit When 0 The pass reached the end of its units, whatever the counts 2 A setup it cannot use: an unknown kind, models that do not fill the kind's roles, a model or keys file it cannot read, no review clone, no gateway address, a model name the gateway rejects, or a task folder this liulab-llms cannot read. One line on stderr says which 3 The pass stopped: at its ceiling, at a provider's balance or cap, or because a provider or the gateway was unavailable. Or another process holds the task, and message names it

docs.title: Resume a pass
docs.text: Run the same command again. There is no resume option. Every unit answered before comes back from the gateway's cache at no cost, and cache_hits counts them. After a stop at the ceiling, raise --ceiling-usd and run it again.

docs.title: See where a kind stands
docs.text:
seqforge pass status <kind>

This reads the kind's task and the review clone and prints one JSON object. It sends nothing to the gateway, so it works with the gateway down, and wherever the task folder is. It takes --task DIR and --reviews DIR as pass start does.

Field Value kind, task The kind, and the task folder units How many units any pass of the kind has recorded counts Each unit's current ending: settled, unsettled, refused or dropped, a person's review included. Then the units whose latest outcome is unfinished or held. A unit settled once and unfinished in a later pass counts under both passes Every pass of the kind, oldest first

Each pass gives its pass_id, label, kind_version, models, store_build, ceiling_usd, stopped, its counts, and what it spent: spent_usd, first_cost_usd, requests and cache_hits. ended is false for a pass that was killed before it ended.

Each pass's per_unit gives its cost and time per unit, over the units that called a model in that pass. An answer from the cache counts, and a held unit or one the pass never started does not. units says how many there were. For each of spent_usd (dollars paid now), first_cost_usd (dollars when each answer was first paid), requests and seconds, it gives the total, the median and the 90th percentile (p90).

Exit When 0 The report is on stdout 2 An unknown kind, no review clone, or a folder that holds no task. One line on stderr says which 3 A running pass holds the task, and message names it. That pass's stderr is the live view

docs.title: Send the hard units to a stronger model
docs.text:
After a pass, rerun only the units that did not settle, on a stronger model:

seqforge pass start <kind> --ceiling-usd 5 --only unsettled,refused --model writer=deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro

A unit a person has already reviewed is left out, as long as its inputs have not changed since the review.

docs.title: File units for review
docs.text:
A unit that ends unsettled or refused waits in its kind's review queue until a person answers it. People answer in the lab's private review repo, one GitHub issue for each unit:

seqforge review file <kind>

This files five units from the queue, in the kind's own review order. Each new issue asks a person for a few minutes, so keep the number small. --count sets a different number.

A unit is never filed twice for the same inputs, whether its first issue is still open or closed. When a unit's inputs change, a pass answers it again, and it can then be filed again. A unit whose inputs changed after its latest pass waits: it is filed once a pass has answered the new inputs. The command holds the task until it has filed everything, so a second review file on the same task folder exits 3. Two commands on different task folders, such as on two machines, are not kept apart and can file the same unit twice.

Each issue shows:

  • the unit's records, with links
  • each pass's answer, with the models that gave it and its stamp
  • each check that the answer failed, with the check's message
  • the boxes to tick: one answer to start from, which is a pass's answer or one that the kind's code offers; the kind's questions about single items; and the reasons to drop the unit

To answer, tick the boxes, then close the issue. Close it as completed to keep your answer, or as not planned to drop the unit with the reasons you ticked. A hidden line at the top of the issue holds the kind, the unit's key, its inputs and the answers you can start from. Do not edit it.

Each issue has the label review:<kind>, and a label check:<name> for each check that its answer failed. Filter the issue list by a label to see one kind or one check together. The command makes each label that the repo does not have yet.

The options:

Option What it does --count How many units to file. Default 5 --task DIR The task folder. Default: seqforge/passes/<kind>/ in the current folder --reviews DIR The review repo's clone, if SEQFORGE_REVIEWS does not name it. The issues go to the GitHub repo that its origin names

stdout carries one JSON object: kind, task, filed, which lists each filed unit's key and the issue's url, and unfiled, the number of units in the queue that are still not filed.

Exit When 0 It filed what it could, up to --count 2 A setup it cannot use: an unknown kind, no review clone, no task in the folder, no gh, or a clone whose origin is not on GitHub. One line on stderr says which 3 Another process holds the task, such as a running pass or another review file, and message names it. Or a GitHub call failed: stopped is github_failed, and filed lists what was filed before it. Run the command again to file the rest

docs.title: Read reviews back
docs.text:
Once people have closed issues, read their answers back:

seqforge review read <kind>

This reads each closed issue of the kind that has not been read back yet:

  • An issue closed as completed stores the answer that its ticks make. The review records the GitHub login of the person who closed the issue, and the pass whose answer they started from.
  • An issue closed as not planned stores a drop, with the reasons ticked as its note.

Each review goes into the kind's file in the reviews/ folder of the clone. From then on the unit counts as settled or dropped, and a pass leaves it out while its inputs stay the same. The command does not open the task, so it works while a pass runs.

If the ticks make no answer, or the answer fails one of the kind's checks, nothing is stored. The same is true if a ticked box's hidden marker was edited and cannot be read. The command adds a comment to the issue that says why, reopens it, and goes on to the next issue. Fix the ticks, then close the issue again.

If the unit's inputs changed after the issue was filed, its answer is for inputs that the unit no longer has, so nothing is stored. The command says so in a comment, adds the label inputs-changed, and leaves the issue closed. A pass answers the new inputs, and the unit is filed again if it still needs a person.

If the unit's inputs are missing for now, the unit is held. The command stores nothing, and it does not comment on the issue, label it or reopen it. It lists the unit under held, and the next run reads the issue again.

Each issue is read back only once. After storing, the command commits the kind's review file, and nothing else in the clone, then pushes it. If another clone pushed first, the command pulls, and git's union merge keeps the lines from both. If the push still fails, the reviews stay committed in the clone, and the next run pushes them.

The options:

Option What it does --reviews DIR The review repo's clone, if SEQFORGE_REVIEWS does not name it. The reviews are stored, committed and pushed there. The issues are read from the GitHub repo that its origin names

stdout carries one JSON object:

Field Value kind The kind answered Each stored answer: the unit's key, the issue's url, who closed it, and accepted_pass, the pass whose answer they started from, or null for an answer the kind's code offered dropped Each stored drop: key, url, who and note reopened Each reopened issue: key, url, and the reason that its comment gives inputs_changed Each issue left closed because its unit's inputs changed: key and url held Each issue left for a later run because its unit's inputs are missing for now: key and url pushed true if it pushed, false if the push failed, or null if there was nothing to push stopped, message Only on exit 3: github_failed or git_failed, and the message from GitHub or git Exit When 0 It read back each closed issue that it could, and reopened none 2 A setup it cannot use: an unknown kind, no review clone, no gh, a clone whose origin is not on GitHub, or a kind that reads liulab-data's store when the store cannot be opened. One line on stderr says which 3 A GitHub call or a git step failed. The reviews stored before it are committed in the clone. Run the command again to read the rest and push. Exit 3 wins over exit 4 4 It reopened at least one issue, so a person has to answer it again

docs.title: Set up the review repo
docs.text:
The lab set up the review repo once, with gh. These are the steps, for the record or for a new copy:

gh repo create liuhlab/seqforge-review --private \
  --description "Reviews of seqforge units: one issue per unit, answered by ticking boxes and closing"
gh repo clone liuhlab/seqforge-review
cd seqforge-review
mkdir -p reviews
printf '*.jsonl merge=union\n' > reviews/.gitattributes
# Write a short README.md that says what the repo is for, then:
git add README.md reviews/.gitattributes
git commit -m "Set up the review repo"
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
gh label create hand-check --repo liuhlab/seqforge-review \
  --description "The benchmark's hand-check of a settled unit"

The reviews/ folder holds one review file for each kind, one line for each review. Each person's clone adds lines to the same files, so merge=union tells git to keep the lines from both sides of a merge, not to stop on a conflict. The hand-check label is for the benchmark's own check of settled units. The review commands make every other label when they first need it.

docs.title: The study workflow
docs.text:
A study is one piece of research: the experiments one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet. Public archives do not store studies. GEO (the Gene Expression Omnibus, a public archive of sequencing data) stores Series. One paper's data can span several Series, and a Series links to papers and to other Series that do not all belong to the same study.

This page gives the chain of steps that takes one study from its database records to two files:

  • bounds.yaml holds the study's bounds: its name, the Series that belong to it, its papers, and each linked record that was left out, with the reason. A study is whole Series. No step splits a Series by sample.
  • reading.yaml holds the study reading: what was done to each sample, and how the samples relate. There is one reading per study.

The chain is built and checked on the standard set, a fixed list of 50 small GEO studies. For those 50, both files sit in the study's folder, evals/standard-set/<ID>/. <ID> is the Series the study was picked by, such as GSE100021.

The work is planned in stages, and two steps are not built yet. Stage 5 builds the reader, and stage 6 runs the whole chain once with no person involved. Each of those steps already has its name, its input and its output below.

docs.title: The steps in order
docs.text:
# Step Command Reads Writes State 1 Bound the study seqforge pass start study-bounds, then seqforge study write-bounds The records linked to the study, and its papers' abstracts bounds.yaml Built 2 Check the bounds seqforge study check-bounds <file> One bounds.yaml No file. It prints whether the file is accepted Built 3 Read the study Command not named yet The study's bounds.yaml, its records and its papers reading.yaml Not built yet. Stage 5 builds it 4 Check the reading seqforge study check-reading <file> One reading.yaml No file. It prints whether the file is accepted Built 5 Derive the relations seqforge study relations <reading.yaml> One reading.yaml No file. It prints the relations Built 6 Run the chain unattended Command not named yet About 2,000 GEO Series For each study, a bounds.yaml and a reading.yaml, or the reason the study stopped Not built yet. Stage 6 builds it

Steps 1 to 5 handle one study. Step 6 is the same chain, run over many studies at once.

The 50 studies of the standard set got their own bounds before step 1 was built, from commands that are now retired. How the standard set got its bounds lists them. The checks run like this, on one study of the standard set:

seqforge study check-bounds evals/standard-set/<ID>/bounds.yaml
seqforge study check-reading evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.yaml
seqforge study relations evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.yaml

docs.title: Rules that every step follows
docs.text:
One format at a time. Every bounds.yaml and every reading.yaml starts with the line format: <number>. Each check accepts only the current number. It rejects a file that has any other number, and its message names the number that it expected. A change to a format rewrites every existing file in the same change, so no file stays behind in an older format.

A person never blocks a step. A model writes, a model checks, and a person can read the results on a view-only page on the side. No step waits for a person's answer. A study that the chain cannot settle keeps its best answer with its probability, or the chain lists the study with the reason it stopped. If a person does answer a question while checking, the answer is saved as a small plain file: the question, the study, the answer, who gave it and when.

No step reads sequencing data. Every step works from database records and papers.

docs.title: 1. Bound the study
docs.text:
Bounding is drawing a study from its linked records. The bounding job runs a pass of the study-bounds kind, which asks a model the same kind of question once for each study and keeps each answer in the pass's task folder. Passes and reviews describes passes. A study is named by the GEO Series it starts from. With no --keys file, the pass runs the 50 studies of the standard set.

seqforge pass start study-bounds --ceiling-usd 0.1
seqforge study write-bounds --out evals/standard-set --name job-bounds.yaml

What it reads. The job reads liulab-data, the lab package that stores the archive records and the papers, from LABDATA_STORE and LABDATA_PAPERS. For each study it gathers the linked group: the starting Series, every Series one link away from it, and every paper that those Series link. Four kinds of link count: a SuperSeries and its sub-Series, a shared BioProject, two BioProjects under one umbrella BioProject, and a shared paper. A reanalysis link counts for nothing, and so does a paper that only a BioProject links.

How it decides. Code keeps the starting Series, or each sub-Series when the study starts from a SuperSeries, and it leaves every SuperSeries out. Jev, a model that answers yes/no questions with a probability, is asked about each other Series and each paper twice: once as written, once reversed. Jev reads the records and each paper's title, journal, date and abstract, and never a full paper. A record is in the study when Jev's answer as written is more likely yes than no. Each claim is inferred, and its text gives Jev's p(yes) to each of the two questions. A kept paper has no probability in the file, so the task keeps it.

What it writes. seqforge study write-bounds --out <folder> writes each study's answer as <folder>/<ID>/bounds.yaml, or under the name that --name gives. It never overwrites a file. For the standard set, the job's file is job-bounds.yaml, beside the set's own bounds.yaml. Each study ends in one of three ways:

Ending When File Settled Jev's two answers agree on every record Written Unsettled Jev's two answers disagree on a record Written, with each probability Refused The group holds more than 50 Series, or the bounds fail the format check None. write-bounds prints the reason, such as group too large

docs.title: How the standard set got its bounds
docs.text: This is history: these commands are retired. A small model drafted each of the 50 studies' bounds in a pass of the standard-set-bounds kind. The standard-set draft command wrote each answer as <ID>/draft.yaml. The standard-set judge command asked a large model about one draft and wrote <ID>/verdict.yaml, <ID>/bounds.yaml and <ID>/study.yaml. seqforge standard-set list still prints one JSON object per study. The standard set's own page says what each file holds.

docs.title: 2. Check the bounds
docs.text:
seqforge study check-bounds <file> reads one bounds.yaml and nothing else. It opens no archive and calls no model. It prints one JSON object that says whether the file is accepted, and for each problem it names the field and the reason. It exits 0 for an accepted file, 3 for a rejected file and 2 for a file that it cannot read.

The check asks only whether the file is in the current format. It does not judge whether the bounds are right. The bounding job never writes a file that the check rejects: it ends the study refused. What the reader does with a rejected file, stage 5 decides.

docs.title: 3. Read the study
docs.text:
Not built yet. Stage 5 builds this step, and its command is not named yet.

The reader writes one study's reading from three inputs: the study's bounds.yaml, the records of the Series in those bounds, and the study's papers. It writes one reading.yaml.

A reading has one row per sample. The row says which biosample and which donor the sample came from, which assay was run, and what the library targets or which kind of control library it is. It also holds general attributes such as species and tissue. The reading names the study's factors, the labels that the study varied on purpose, such as a treatment. Each statement in the file is a claim. A claim says how it is backed, for example by a passage quoted from a record or a paper, and it carries a probability.

Until the reader exists, the only readings are worked examples for a few studies of the standard set. A model wrote each of them.

docs.title: 4. Check the reading
docs.text:
seqforge study check-reading <file> reads one reading.yaml and nothing else, and it accepts or rejects the file. For each problem it names the field and the reason.

The check looks at the structure of the file. Every sample must have every label, every claim must say how it is backed in exactly one way, and every passage that a claim cites, for it or against it, must be in the file. A file that writes an ontology id must name where its ids came from. The check does not compare a quote with the record that the quote came from. That comparison needs the records, so it belongs to step 3.

docs.title: 5. Derive the relations
docs.text:
seqforge study relations <reading.yaml> reads one reading and prints how its samples relate. Code works the relations out from the labels in the reading each time the command runs. No file stores them, so a relation is never out of date with its reading.

The command prints five kinds of relation:

Relation Meaning Contrasts Two groups of samples that differ in one factor, with the other factors equal. One group is at the baseline, such as untreated Replicates Samples that have the same assay, the same target, the same control type and the same level of every factor Series Samples in order along a factor whose levels have an order, such as time points or doses. This kind of series is not a GEO Series Shared biosamples Samples that were made from the same biosample, such as two assays on one piece of tissue Signal-to-control pairs A library that has a target, paired with its background control library, such as an input library, made from the same material

docs.title: 6. Run the chain unattended
docs.text:
Not built yet. Stage 6 builds this step, and its command is not named yet.

This step runs the chain once over about 2,000 GEO Series, which is about 1% of the sequencing Series in GEO. The Series are drawn from liulab-data's store, and the 50 studies of the standard set are kept out. The chain bounds and reads every study with no person involved.

For each study the run writes a bounds.yaml and a reading.yaml, or it lists the study with the reason it stopped. Every study ends as settled, unsettled or refused, as Passes and reviews defines those endings. No study is sent to a person.

docs.title: Files that exist today
docs.text: Files from the hand work lists every bounds file, worked reading and verdict made so far, with where each is, its format and who made it.

docs.title: The two artifacts
docs.text: seqforge produces two files, and almost every design argument reduces to why they are two files and not one.

docs.title: A fact and a choice are different things
docs.text:
Those molecules went through that flowcell and produced those bytes: a fact, already in the past. You are going to align it to a particular genome and count particular things: a choice, which someone else could defensibly make differently, and which you will redo next year with a better aligner.

Facts and choices have different lifetimes, so they get different files:

dataset manifest processing manifest answers what the data is what to do with it authority the bytes, and the people who ran the experiment you how many exactly one per dataset as many as you like can it change? no — named by its hash, written once yes, freely

docs.title: Why not one file?
docs.text:
Because the moment they share a file, re-processing edits the truth. Re-run with a different genome build and you edit the file — but nothing about the data changed. You did. And the file's identity changed with it: if you were using its hash to say "this is that dataset", you have silently claimed it is a different one. Do that across ten thousand datasets and the corpus's provenance is fiction.

So the rule is absolute: changing your mind about processing must never change the dataset's hash. A test compiles one dataset three ways and asserts the hash never moves.

docs.title: Same source, different flags
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    D["<span style='color:#fff'>dataset manifest<br/><code>hash: a3f9…</code><br/><i>never changes</i></span>"]

    D --> C1["compose"]
    D --> C2["compose"]
    D --> C3["compose"]

    P1["processing:<br/>human genome<br/>count exons"] --> C1
    P2["processing:<br/>human genome<br/>count introns too"] --> C2
    P3["processing:<br/>newer genome build"] --> C3

    C1 --> R1["run a1b2…"]
    C2 --> R2["run c3d4…"]
    C3 --> R3["run e5f6…"]

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class D artifact

Three runs, three identities, one unchanged fact at the top. Each run's identity is computed from everything that went into it — dataset, choices, knowledge base version, pipeline module version — so runs cannot collide, and any run traces back to exactly what produced it.

-O2 does not get to edit your source code. A processing manifest does not get to edit the dataset manifest.

docs.title: The line: parsing versus counting
docs.text:
How to parse the reads — where the barcode starts, how long the UMI is, which strand — is decided by the bytes. You cannot instruct it, and neither can a paper. It lives in the knowledge base.

What to count — genes, or genes-plus-introns, against which genome — is a choice. It lives in the processing manifest, and you can instruct it.

The two sets do not overlap. Not "your instruction is deprioritized if it conflicts with the bytes" — there is no way to write the conflicting instruction down. You have no vocabulary in which to say "the barcode is 10 bases long".

That is why seqforge can read your instructions without ever trusting them: it lets you talk only about things you are entitled to decide.

docs.title: One project, one or more datasets
docs.text:
The table above says "exactly one dataset manifest per dataset", and a dataset is one chemistry. A real study is often not that: a single archive series can mix 10x v2 and v3 libraries, and a manifest that averaged the two would describe neither.

So a heterogeneous project splits into assays — one per chemistry, decided from the bytes, never by you. Each assay is an ordinary dataset: its own immutable manifest.yaml, its own hash, its own Snakefile, under its own seqforge/<assay>/ directory. Nothing about the single-dataset story changes; there are simply several of them.

Two files tie the project back together at the top level:

  • sample_metadata.tsv — one row per sample across every assay (sample id, accession, assay, organism, files): the flat "one study" view.
  • project.yaml — the index of which assays exist, their chemistry and sample counts, and where each one's manifest and pipeline live.

A uniform project — most of them — is the simplest case: one assay, the flat layout of the rest of this guide, plus that top-level sample_metadata.tsv.

docs.title: Filenames are not evidence
docs.text:
_1 and _2 mean nothing. Those numbers come from whatever wrote the files — an archive's unpacking tool numbering them in the order it found them, a sequencer's demultiplexer, a script someone wrote once and forgot. SRR123_1.fastq.gz is not "read 1" in any biological sense. It might hold the barcodes, it might hold the RNA, it might be missing.

So seqforge never trusts the name. It opens the files and looks.

docs.title: Cheap things first
docs.text:
Answers are ranked by cost. seqforge starts at the bottom and climbs only when it has to:

flowchart TD
    R0["<b>0 · the prose</b><br/>'10x 3′ v3.1', from a paper or database<br/><i>a hypothesis — never a conclusion</i>"]
    R1["<b>1 · the filenames</b><br/><i>a weak hint, never decisive</i>"]
    R2["<span style='color:#fff'><b>2 · the shape of the reads</b><br/>read lengths, which stretches are random,<br/>which are fixed, which barcodes repeat<br/><i>free — we are reading the bytes anyway</i></span>"]
    R3["<span style='color:#fff'><b>3 · check one barcode list</b><br/>do these barcodes appear in 10x's<br/>published list of real barcodes?<br/><i>the first rung that costs anything</i></span>"]
    R7["<b>7 · ask a human</b><br/><i>expensive — and that is the point</i>"]

    R0 --> R1 --> R2 --> R3
    R3 -->|"a genuine tie that<br/>would change the output"| R7
    R3 -->|"decided"| DONE["<span style='color:#fff'>dataset manifest</span>"]

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    classDef output fill:#37474f,stroke:#263238
    class R2,R3 artifact
    class DONE output

Rungs 0 to 3 cost well under a second and settle almost everything. The numbering leaves room for intermediate rungs — a broader barcode search, a genome sketch, a trial alignment — so an ambiguity surviving rung 3 goes straight to a human.

docs.title: The prose proposes; the bytes decide
docs.text:
Notice where the prose sits: at the bottom, as rung 0.

That is not disrespect. Metadata turns an open-ended search ("what could this be?") into a cheap yes/no check ("the page says 10x v3; do these barcodes match v3's list?"). Trust it enough to skip the search, never enough to skip the check.

If the page and the bytes disagree, that is reported as a conflict, and the bytes win on the factual question.

docs.title: What the bytes give away for free
docs.text:
While streaming a bounded sample:

  • Which stretches are fixed and which are random. The same base at position 30 in almost every read is adapter, not data. Long runs of T are a poly-T tail.
  • Which stretches repeat. Barcodes recur, because you sequence the same cell many times; UMIs and RNA are nearly all distinct. This tells barcodes from UMIs with no barcode list at all.
  • Whether someone already trimmed the file. A sequencer produces reads of exactly one length. If a technical read has several, a trimming tool ran before upload — and trimming tools do not know a barcode from an adapter. Offsets may have shifted. That is a refusal, not a warning.

docs.title: Roles are solved, not guessed
docs.text: Once seqforge knows what a technology expects — "one 28-base read holding a barcode, one variable-length read holding RNA" — it tries every way of matching files to slots and keeps the arrangement best supported by the evidence. The technology's score is its best arrangement's score, so a swapped _1/_2 gives an identical answer.

docs.title: Reading a whole file is a bug
docs.text:
Every look at a FASTQ is bounded: by default the first 2,000 reads and at most 256 MB decompressed, whichever comes first. Two thousand is enough — the chemistry a file resolves to is invariant from a thousand reads up past two hundred thousand — and it is a floor, not a ceiling: raise --max-reads to sample more of a full-size file when you want to. A code path that can stream a whole multi-gigabyte file is a defect even if today's file is small — because eventually it won't be, and by then the path is load-bearing. A test hands the probe a 128 MB file and asserts it reads a bounded prefix and stops.

Note the units: reads and bytes, never seconds. Wall-clock depends on the disk, the compression level, and whether the machine is busy. It is a consequence, not a constraint.

docs.title: When it refuses
docs.text: The most useful thing seqforge does is stop. A tool that always produces an answer is only trustworthy if you check the answer, and at ten thousand datasets nobody checks. So it is built to fail loudly where a normal pipeline fails silently.

docs.title: Three ways it can end
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    START["a dataset"] --> Q{"can code decide it?"}
    Q -->|yes| OK["<span style='color:#fff'><b>manifest</b><br/>exit 0</span>"]
    Q -->|"something is structurally wrong"| BLK["<span style='color:#fff'><b>blocker</b><br/>exit 3<br/><i>this cannot be processed</i></span>"]
    Q -->|"a real question only<br/>a human can settle"| ASK["<span style='color:#fff'><b>question</b><br/>exit 4<br/><i>tell me, and I'll continue</i></span>"]

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    classDef blocked fill:#b71c1c,stroke:#7f0000
    classDef ask fill:#bf360c,stroke:#7f2400
    class OK artifact
    class BLK blocked
    class ASK ask

A refusal is an exit code, not a warning in a log. Code decides whether processing may proceed; the language model never gets a vote, and at most helps phrase the question.

Every blocker carries a reason and a remedy you can act on. "Could not process" is not a remedy. "The barcode read is missing — re-fetch including technical reads, or pull the submitter's original files" is.

docs.title: The failures worth catching are the quiet ones
docs.text:
Loud failures take care of themselves: a corrupt file explodes and you notice. These do not.

The wrong strand. About half the reads land unassigned, and the matrix just looks like a thin dataset. Public metadata essentially never states the strand.

A trimmed barcode file. A trimming tool ran before upload. Most reads are still the right length, so the geometry checks pass — but some shifted, so the barcode is read from the wrong position and those cells are dropped.

The wrong genome. A worm dataset against the human genome barely maps: loud, therefore fine. The same mistake between two similar genomes is silent, and yields a plausible matrix in the wrong coordinate space.

Counting only exons on a nuclear sample. Nuclei are full of unspliced RNA sitting in introns; count only exons and you throw it away. We measured 40.7% of a nuclear library, gone. The chemistry is byte-identical to the whole-cell version, so the reads cannot tell you which you have.

Every one of them exits 0.

docs.title: Never ask a question you don't need answered
docs.text:
Refusing is expensive too: a system that questions you constantly is one you route around, and then it protects nobody.

Don't ask if the answer can't change anything. Two versions of the 10x chemistry may be indistinguishable from the reads. If they produce identical settings, record both names and move on. This is computed, not assumed: a check over every pair asserts that "indistinguishable" and "identical settings" agree.

Don't ask if you can afford every answer. Nuclear-versus-whole-cell is unanswerable from the reads — so count all five ways at once. One alignment, five counting rules, one pass. Download and alignment dominate the cost so completely that the extra counting is close to free.

flowchart LR
    Q["'is this cells or nuclei?'<br/>— unanswerable from the reads"]
    Q --> BAD["<span style='color:#fff'>ask the human<br/><i>exit 4</i></span>"]
    Q --> GOOD["<span style='color:#fff'>count all five ways<br/><i>exit 0</i></span>"]

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef ask fill:#bf360c,stroke:#7f2400
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class BAD ask
    class GOOD artifact

Save the interruptions for things that are genuinely exclusive — a genome, an aligner — where you really do have to choose one.

docs.title: The bounds file
docs.text:
A study is one piece of research: the experiments one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet. Public archives do not store studies. GEO stores Series, and a Series links to papers and to other Series. Not everything linked belongs to the same study.

A study's bounds say what belongs to it: which GEO Series, and which papers. The bounds file writes that down, one file per study, as YAML. This page is all you need to read one.

seqforge study check-bounds evals/standard-set/GSE101112/bounds.yaml

The 50 studies of the standard set each have one, at evals/standard-set/<ID>/bounds.yaml.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
format: 1
study: GSE101112
models:
  bounds: example/model-a
  probabilities: example/model-b
series:
- id: GSE101112
  quoted: [1]
  p: 0.97
papers:
- pmid:31742554
left_out:
- id: pmid:33294943
  inferred: Software paper that uses the dataset only as test data
  see: [2]
  p: 0.9
- id: pmid:32884834
  unknown: Nothing that was read says whether it made new data
  p: null
reason: The 2019 paper made and reports the data held in this Series.
passages:
  1:
    paper: pmid:31742554
    section: Data availability
    quote: "RNA-seq data have been deposited in GEO under accession GSE101112"
  2:
    record: GSE101112
    field: Series_citation
    quote: "A tool paper that lists this Series among its examples"

This example is made up to show every part. Its quotes, numbers and model names are not real.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text:
Every field below is required. A file with any other field is rejected.

Field Holds format The whole number 1. See When the format changes. study The study's name: the GEO Series it was picked by, such as GSE101112. models Who wrote the file. bounds is the model that drew the bounds. probabilities is the model that gave the p values. Either may be null. series The Series that belong to the study. At least one. Each is a claim, and its id is written GSE<number>. papers The papers that report the study, each written pmid:<number>. May be empty. left_out Each linked Series or paper that does not belong. Each is a claim. reason One line saying why these Series and papers are one study. Cannot be blank. passages The quotes that back the claims, each under its number. May be empty: {}.

A study is whole Series. A Series is in the study or it is left out. No field names some of a Series' samples. Telling apart the experiments inside one Series is a later step's job, not the bounds'.

For a SuperSeries, series lists its sub-Series, and the SuperSeries itself is in left_out. So the study's name is not always one of its series.

A record is placed once. It is in series, in papers or in left_out, never in two of them and never twice.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
A claim is one decision the file makes: one Series kept, or one record left out. Each entry of series and of left_out is a claim. A claim holds the record's id, exactly one backing mark, and p.

Field Holds id The record: a Series such as GSE101112, or a paper such as pmid:33294943. Cannot be blank. quoted Backing mark. A source says it: the numbers of the passages that say so. inferred Backing mark. No passage says it outright: a short text saying how it was worked out. unknown Backing mark. What was read does not say: a short note. see Optional, and not beside quoted: the numbers of the passages the claim rests on. p A number from 0 to 1, or null. Required.

The rules for a claim:

  • It has exactly one of quoted, inferred and unknown. None is rejected, and so are two.
  • quoted lists at least one passage.
  • Every number in quoted and in see must be a passage in the file.
  • The text after inferred or unknown cannot be blank.

In left_out, the backing is also the reason the record does not belong. For an inferred claim that is its text. For a quoted claim it is what the passages say. There is no separate reason field.

p is the chance that the claim as written is right, as a model judged it. null means that no model has given one yet. It does not mean the claim is in doubt. When any claim has a number, models.probabilities must name the model that gave it.

A reading file writes its claims and its passages the same way, so the two kinds of file read alike. A claim in a reading has one more backing mark, na, which the bounds do not use, and more fields for what the claim says.

docs.title: Passages
docs.text:
A quote is written once in the file, however many claims it backs. passages is keyed by number: a whole number, 1 or more. Each passage holds the quote and where it was read, in one of two ways.

Field Holds quote The words, copied from the source. record and field For a quote from a GEO record: the record, and the field of it. paper and section For a quote from a paper: the paper, and the section of it.

docs.title: The 50 files of the standard set
docs.text:
The 50 studies were drawn before quotes and probabilities were part of the format. Their files were converted, so in each of them:

  • every claim is inferred, and its text is the reason the model wrote when it drew the study;
  • every p is null, and so is models.probabilities;
  • models.bounds names the model whose bounds became the study's;
  • passages is empty.

docs.title: The check
docs.text:
seqforge study check-bounds <file> reads one file and prints one JSON object:

{
  "file": "bounds.yaml",
  "format": 1,
  "valid": false,
  "problems": [
    {"field": "series[0].quoted", "reason": "passage 7 does not exist"},
    {"field": "split_samples", "reason": "not a field of the format"}
  ]
}

It exits 0 for a valid file, 3 for a rejected one, and 2 for a file it cannot read. A file that is not UTF-8 text cannot be read. Each problem names the field and the reason. series[0] is the first entry of series.

A key that one mapping writes twice is rejected, and the problem names the key. Plain YAML keeps the last of the two and reports nothing, so a repeated field would go unseen.

A value has the type that this page writes for it. A number in quotes, such as p: "0.5", is rejected, and so is true where a number belongs.

The check asks only whether the file is well formed. It does not open GEO, and it does not judge whether the bounds are right.

docs.title: When the format changes
docs.text:
There is one format at a time. format is a whole number, and the check accepts only the current one. A file with another number is rejected, and the message names the number the check expected.

A change to the format raises the number and rewrites every existing file in the same change. No file stays behind in an older format, and git history is the only record of the old form.

docs.title: The reading file
docs.text:
A study is one piece of research: the experiments one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet. The bounds file says which GEO Series and papers belong to a study. The study's reading says what each sequenced sample is: the species, the tissue, the treatment, the assay, and which label the study varied between its samples. Each statement comes with the words that back it, the words that speak against it where the sources disagree, and a probability. The reading file writes that down, one file per study, as YAML. This page is all you need to read one.

seqforge study check-reading reading.yaml
seqforge study relations reading.yaml

The first command checks a file against this page. The second command prints what the reading implies between its samples, such as replicates and contrasts.

docs.title: The file at a glance
docs.text:
A reading file has five parts. The arrows show how one part points at another.

flowchart TD
    HEAD["<b>header</b><br/><code>format</code> · <code>study</code><br/><code>models</code> · <code>read</code><br/><code>ontology_snapshot</code><br/><i>which study, who wrote it,<br/>what was read, where ids came from</i>"]
    SHARED["<b>shared</b><br/>the claims every sample has"]
    SAMPLES["<span style='color:#fff'><b>samples</b><br/>one row per sequenced sample:<br/>the claims of its own</span>"]
    FACTORS["<b>factors</b><br/>the labels the study varied:<br/>levels, baseline, ordered or not"]
    PASSAGES["<b>passages</b><br/>the numbered quotes,<br/>each with where it was read"]
    SRC[("GEO records<br/>and papers")]

    HEAD ~~~ SHARED
    SHARED -->|"a row's claim replaces<br/>the shared claim"| SAMPLES
    SAMPLES -->|"<code>level</code> names one<br/>of the factor's levels"| FACTORS
    SHARED -->|"<code>quoted</code>, <code>see</code> and<br/><code>against</code> list passage numbers"| PASSAGES
    SAMPLES --> PASSAGES
    FACTORS --> PASSAGES
    PASSAGES -->|"<code>record</code> or <code>paper</code>"| SRC

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class SAMPLES artifact

Read it from the samples outward. A sample's claims are its own row plus whatever shared adds. A claim that is backed by a source gives passage numbers, and each passage names the record or the paper that holds the quote. A claim that a source contradicts names that passage too, under against. A claim on a label that the study varied also names its level.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
A liver study of two ages. Each age has one pull-down library and the input library made from the same chromatin. The paper gives the old mice a different age from the records.

format: 2
study: GSE900001
models:
  reading: example/model-a
  probabilities: example/model-b
read: [records, abstract]
read_detail: The Series, its four samples, and the abstract of the one paper.
ontology_snapshot: {source: example ontology snapshot, date: 2026-11-21}

passages:
  1: {record: GSE900001, field: Series_overall_design, quote: "H3K27me3 ChIP-seq and input from liver of young and old male mice"}
  2: {record: each_sample, field: Sample_organism_ch1, quote: "Mus musculus"}
  3: {record: [GSM9000001, GSM9000002], field: Sample_characteristics_ch1, quote: "age: 2 months"}
  4: {record: [GSM9000003, GSM9000004], field: Sample_characteristics_ch1, quote: "age: 24 months"}
  5: {record: [GSM9000002, GSM9000004], field: Sample_characteristics_ch1, quote: "antibody: none (input)"}
  6: {paper: "pmid:99000001", section: abstract, quote: "livers were collected at noon from C57BL/6J mice"}
  7: {paper: "pmid:99000001", section: abstract, quote: "old mice were 22 months of age"}

factors:
  age:
    levels: [young, old]
    baseline: young
    ordered: true
    quoted: [1]
    p: 0.97

shared:
  donor:             {unknown: "No record says which animal a library came from", p: 0.8}
  assay:             {text: ChIP-seq, term: "EFO:0002692", quoted: [1], p: 0.99}
  target:            {text: H3K27me3, quoted: [1], p: 0.98}
  control_type:      {na: "A pull-down library, not a background control", p: 0.97}
  species:           {text: Mus musculus, term: "NCBITaxon:10090", quoted: [2], p: 0.99}
  sex:               {text: male, term: male, quoted: [1], p: 0.97}
  development_stage: {text: adult, inferred: "A mouse of 2 months or more is an adult", see: [3, 4], p: 0.9}
  tissue:            {text: liver, term: "UBERON:0002107", quoted: [1], p: 0.98}
  cell_type:         {na: "Whole tissue, no cell type was isolated", p: 0.9}
  cell_line:         {na: "Tissue taken from the animal", p: 0.99}
  disease:           {text: healthy, term: "PATO:0000461", inferred: "No disease is named", p: 0.85}
  genotype:          {unknown: "No record gives a genotype", p: 0.9}
  strain:            {text: C57BL/6J, quoted: [6], p: 0.95}
  treatment:         {na: "No treatment is described", p: 0.9}
  dose:              {na: "No treatment", p: 0.9}
  duration:          {na: "No treatment", p: 0.9}
  time_of_day:       {text: noon, quoted: [6], p: 0.9}

samples:
  GSM9000001:
    biosample:    {id: B1, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 2 months, value: 2, unit: month, level: young, quoted: [3], p: 0.97}
  GSM9000002:
    biosample:    {id: B1, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 2 months, value: 2, unit: month, level: young, quoted: [3], p: 0.97}
    target:       {na: "Input chromatin, no pull-down", p: 0.98}
    control_type: {text: input, quoted: [5], p: 0.98}
  GSM9000003:
    biosample:    {id: B2, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 24 months, value: 24, unit: month, level: old, quoted: [4], against: [7], p: 0.9}
  GSM9000004:
    biosample:    {id: B2, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 24 months, value: 24, unit: month, level: old, quoted: [4], against: [7], p: 0.9}
