    target:       {na: "Input chromatin, no pull-down", p: 0.98}
    control_type: {text: input, quoted: [5], p: 0.98}

This example is made up to show every part. Its records, quotes, numbers and model names are not real. It passes the check.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text:
Every field below is required unless the table says otherwise. A file with any other top-level field is rejected.

Field Holds format The whole number 2. See When the format changes. study The study's name: the GEO Series it was picked by, such as GSE100021. models Who wrote the file. reading is the model that read the study. probabilities is the model that gave the p values. Either may be null. read What the model read: one or more of records, abstract and full_text. No other word is accepted. read_detail Optional. One sentence that says which records and which paper. ontology_snapshot Where the file's ontology ids came from, written once: source names the dated snapshot of the ontologies, or the service the ids were looked up in, and date is its date, written 2026-11-21. Required when any claim has a term, except a term on sex, which is a word of this page's own. passages The quotes that back the claims, each under its number. May be empty: {}. factors The labels the study varied on purpose, each under its label. May be empty: {}. shared The claims that every sample has unless its own row says otherwise. May be empty: {}. samples One row per sequenced sample, each under the sample's id, such as GSM2668015. At least one.

docs.title: Passages
docs.text:
A quote is written once in the file, however many claims it backs. passages is keyed by number: a whole number, 1 or more. Each passage holds the quote and where it was read, in one of two ways.

Field Holds quote The words, copied from the source as one unbroken span. record and field For a quote from a GEO record: the record, and the field of it. paper and section For a quote from a paper: the paper, written pmid:<number>, and the section of it.

record takes one of three forms:

  • one record id, such as GSE100021 or GSM2668015;
  • a list of record ids, when each of those records holds the quote in that field;
  • the word each_sample, when every sample record of the study holds the quote in that field.

A record quote is exact: the field holds it character for character. A paper's text comes with markup and broken lines, so a paper quote is exact after the markup is removed and each run of white space is collapsed to one space.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
A claim is one label of one sample: what the label's value is, how that is backed, and how sure the model is. In the example, tissue: {text: liver, ...} is one claim.

Field Holds text The value, in the source's own words. term An ontology id for the value, such as UBERON:0002107. Written only when the match is clear. On treatment only, a list of ids when one sample got several compounds. value For an age, a dose or a duration: the number, or a range as [low, high]. YAML reads 1.7e12 as text, so write 1.7e+12. unit The unit of value, as one word: month, day, hour. level On a label that is a factor: the name of the sample's level. See Factors. id On biosample and donor: a short name made up in the file, such as B1. quoted Backing mark. A source says it: the numbers of the passages that say so. inferred Backing mark. No passage says it outright: a short text saying how it was worked out. unknown Backing mark. What was read does not say: a short note. na Backing mark. The label does not apply to this sample: a short text saying why. see Optional, and not beside quoted: the numbers of the passages the claim rests on. against Optional, beside any backing mark: the numbers of the passages that say otherwise. p A number from 0 to 1, or null. Required.

Only p and one backing mark are required. A claim with any other field is rejected.

The rules for a claim:

  • It has exactly one of quoted, inferred, unknown and na. None is rejected, and so are two.
  • quoted lists at least one passage.
  • Every number in quoted, in see and in against must be a passage in the file.
  • The text after inferred, unknown or na cannot be blank.
  • A quoted claim and an inferred claim say something: each has text or value. A biosample claim and a donor claim may have an id and neither of the two.
  • An unknown claim and an na claim give no value. So neither has text, term, value, unit or level.

The four backing marks answer three questions in turn:

flowchart LR
    A(["Does the label apply<br/>to this sample?"])
    B(["Can its value be told<br/>from what was read?"])
    C(["Does a passage<br/>say it outright?"])
    NA["<b><code>na</code></b><br/>why it does not apply<br/><i>no value</i>"]
    UNK["<b><code>unknown</code></b><br/>a short note<br/><i>no value</i>"]
    Q["<span style='color:#fff'><b><code>quoted</code></b><br/>the passage numbers<br/><i>has a value</i></span>"]
    I["<span style='color:#fff'><b><code>inferred</code></b><br/>how it was worked out<br/><i>has a value</i></span>"]

    A -->|yes| B
    A -->|no| NA
    B -->|yes| C
    B -->|no| UNK
    C -->|yes| Q
    C -->|no| I

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class Q,I artifact

against is for sources that disagree. When the records say one thing and the paper another, the claim writes the value it judges right, backs it as usual, and lists the passages that say otherwise under against. Its p is the chance that the value it wrote is the right one. A passage that the claim merely does not use is not against it: against names a contradiction. A factor is a claim, so a factor can have against too.

unknown and na are different gaps. unknown means that the label has a value and nothing that was read gives it. na means that the label has no value for this sample, such as the cell line of a tissue sample.

p is the chance that the claim as written is right, given what read lists. A model judged it. On an unknown claim, p is the chance that what was read really does not say. null means that no model has given a probability yet. It does not mean the claim is in doubt. When any claim has a number, models.probabilities must name the model that gave it.

A value has the type that this page writes for it. A number in quotes, such as p: "0.5", is rejected, and so is true where a number belongs.

A bounds file writes its claims and its passages the same way.

docs.title: Samples and shared claims
docs.text:
Each row under samples holds the claims of one sample, each under its label. shared holds claims in the same form.

A sample has every claim under shared, except for a label that its own row writes. The row's claim replaces the shared claim whole: no field of the shared claim carries over. In the example, the two input rows replace the shared target and the shared control_type.

After that rule is applied, every sample must have all 18 labels below. A gap is written as unknown or na, so a label that is absent was forgotten, and the check rejects it.

Label Holds biosample The piece of material the library was made from. Its id is required. Two samples with one id were made from the same material. donor The person or animal the material came from. Its id names the individual. na when the material is a pool or has no single individual. assay The kind of sequencing experiment, such as RNA-Seq or ChIP-Seq. Term: EFO, such as EFO:0008896 for RNA-Seq. target What a pull-down enriches: a histone mark or a protein. na for an assay with no pull-down, and for a control library. No term. Never a factor. control_type The kind of background-control library, such as input or IgG. na for every other library. species The species. Term: NCBI Taxonomy, written NCBITaxon:9606. Must be quoted or inferred. sex The sex. Term: one of female, male, hermaphrodite, mixed. age The age, with value and unit. development_stage The stage of life, such as fetal, larval or adult. Term: the stage list of the species (HsapDv, MmusDv, WBls, FBdv). A rat stage has no list and no term. tissue The tissue or organ. Term: UBERON, or WBbt for C. elegans. cell_type The cell type. Term: Cell Ontology (CL). cell_line The cell line. Term: Cellosaurus. disease The disease or disease model. Term: MONDO, or PATO:0000461 for healthy. genotype The genotype, as text. strain The strain, as text. treatment What was applied to the sample. Term: ChEBI for a chemical, or a list of ChEBI ids when one sample got several compounds. A protein keeps its text with no term. dose How much of the treatment, with value and unit for one number. Text alone when no single number applies, such as "per side". duration How long the treatment was applied, with value and unit for one number. Text alone when no single number applies, such as "overnight".

Tissue, cell type and cell line are three labels, and a sample can have a value in each.

Four points of meaning matter when you write or read these labels. The check does not test them.

  • control_type is about background-control libraries only. An input library or an IgG library measures the background of a pull-down. An untreated or wild-type group that the study compares the others with is a comparison baseline, not a control. Its control_type is na, and the factor's baseline names it.
  • duration is the length of the treatment itself. Any other time is an attribute of the study's own. The time from the end of a treatment to the harvest is one example.
  • An untreated sample in a study that treats writes its text. Its treatment says what it got, such as "untreated" or "vehicle (PBS)", and is not na. na on treatment is for a study with no treatment. The route, the side and what a time is measured from stay in text.
  • A pull-down library and its control are tied by the biosample id. No other field ties them. In the example, each input has the id of the pull-down made from the same chromatin. This tie has a known limit. One control library that serves pull-downs made from different material cannot be tied to all of them, because the control has one biosample id.

A row or shared may hold more labels than the 18. Such a label is an attribute of the study's own, such as time_of_day in the example or a harvest time. Its claim has the same form.

docs.title: Factors
docs.text:
A factor is a label that the study varied on purpose, such as the treatment in a drug study or the age in an aging study. factors is keyed by that label. A sample's value is written once, in the sample's claim on the label. The factor adds the list of levels and how they compare.

Field Holds levels The names of the levels, each a short text. For an ordered factor, the order of this list is the order of the levels. baseline The level the study compares the others with. null when the study compares the levels with each other and none is a reference, such as two tissues. Required. ordered true when the levels run along a scale, such as a time course or a dose series. Otherwise false. a backing mark, see, p A factor is a claim too. It is backed by quoted, inferred or unknown.

The rules for a factor:

  • Its label must be a label of every sample. Where the label does not apply to a sample, the sample's claim on it is na.
  • baseline is one of levels, or null.
  • No level is named twice. A level name is text: quote a name that YAML reads as a number, as "0".
  • At least one sample is at each level in levels.
  • A sample's claim on the factor's label names its level in level, with one of the names in levels. Two samples with different text and the same level are at the same level.
  • A claim with no level on a factor's label means that the factor does not cover that sample. An example is a study that varied the genotype among its RNA-Seq samples only.
  • When the claim under shared names a level, a row's claim that replaces it names a level too. A row's claim that is unknown or na is the exception, because it names none.
  • level on a label that is not a factor is rejected.
  • target is never a factor. The relations already keep samples with different targets apart, and a target has no baseline. A factor keyed target is rejected.

docs.title: The check
docs.text:
seqforge study check-reading <file> reads one file and prints one JSON object:

{
  "file": "reading.yaml",
  "format": 2,
  "valid": false,
  "problems": [
    {"field": "samples.GSM9000003.strain", "reason": "missing: every sample has this label, in its own row or under shared"},
    {"field": "shared.assay.quoted", "reason": "passage 7 does not exist"}
  ]
}

It exits 0 for a valid file, 3 for a rejected one, and 2 for a file it cannot read. A file that is not UTF-8 text cannot be read. Each problem names the field and the reason. samples.GSM9000003.strain is the strain claim of that sample.

A key that one mapping writes twice is rejected, and the problem names the key. Plain YAML keeps the last of the two and reports nothing, so a second row for one sample would replace the first unseen.

The check asks only whether the file is well formed. It reads the file alone and opens no record, so it does not look for a quote in its source, and it does not judge whether a claim is right.

docs.title: The relations
docs.text:
A reading does not store which samples are replicates or which groups the study contrasts. Those follow from the claims, so seqforge study relations <file> works them out on every run and writes no file. The command checks the file first and rejects a broken file exactly as check-reading does. For a valid file, the JSON object has one more field, relations.

Three terms define the relations:

  • Two samples have the same assay, the same target or the same control type when the two claims have the same text, or are both na, or are both unknown.
  • A group is the set of samples that have the same assay, target, control type and level on every factor. A group can be one sample.
  • A control library is a sample whose control_type claim is quoted or inferred. A sample whose control type is unknown is not a control library.
  • A signal is a sample whose target claim is quoted or inferred and that is not a control library.
Relation Holds replicates Each group of two or more samples: the same assay, target, control type and level on every factor. contrasts Each pair of groups that have the same assay and target and differ in the level of exactly one factor. Neither group is a control library. One of the two is at the factor's baseline. For a factor with a null baseline, each pair of levels is one contrast. series For each ordered factor: the samples in level order, among the samples that have the same assay, target, control type and level on every other factor. So input libraries and IgG libraries never share a series. A series has at least two levels. shared_biosample Each set of two or more samples with one biosample id. signal_to_control Within one such set: each signal, paired with each control library.

For the example above, the command prints these relations. Samples, factors and levels are listed in the file's order. The picture shows the same relations, and the JSON follows it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph B1["biosample B1 · age: young"]
        S1["<span style='color:#fff'><b>GSM9000001</b><br/>H3K27me3 pull-down<br/><i>signal</i></span>"]
        S2["<b>GSM9000002</b><br/>input<br/><i>its control</i>"]
    end
    subgraph B2["biosample B2 · age: old"]
        S3["<span style='color:#fff'><b>GSM9000003</b><br/>H3K27me3 pull-down<br/><i>signal</i></span>"]
        S4["<b>GSM9000004</b><br/>input<br/><i>its control</i>"]
    end

    S1 ==>|"contrast and series<br/>young to old"| S3
    S2 -.->|"series only<br/>young to old"| S4

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class S1,S3 artifact

Each box is one shared_biosample set. Inside a box, the pull-down library and the input library make one signal_to_control pair. The two pull-down libraries make the one contrast. The two input libraries make a series and no contrast, because a control library is never in a contrast. No group has two samples, so there are no replicates.

{
  "replicates": [],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "factor": "age",
      "baseline": "young",
      "levels": ["young", "old"],
      "samples": {"young": ["GSM9000001"], "old": ["GSM9000003"]},
      "assay": "ChIP-seq",
      "target": "H3K27me3",
      "fixed": {}
    }
  ],
  "series": [
    {
      "factor": "age",
      "assay": "ChIP-seq",
      "target": "H3K27me3",
      "control_type": null,
      "fixed": {},
      "steps": [
        {"level": "young", "samples": ["GSM9000001"]},
        {"level": "old", "samples": ["GSM9000003"]}
      ]
    },
    {
      "factor": "age",
      "assay": "ChIP-seq",
      "target": null,
      "control_type": "input",
      "fixed": {},
      "steps": [
        {"level": "young", "samples": ["GSM9000002"]},
        {"level": "old", "samples": ["GSM9000004"]}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "shared_biosample": [
    {"biosample": "B1", "samples": ["GSM9000001", "GSM9000002"]},
    {"biosample": "B2", "samples": ["GSM9000003", "GSM9000004"]}
  ],
  "signal_to_control": [
    {"biosample": "B1", "signal": "GSM9000001", "control": "GSM9000002"},
    {"biosample": "B2", "signal": "GSM9000003", "control": "GSM9000004"}
  ]
}

In a contrast, levels holds the two levels, with the baseline first when the factor has one. fixed holds the level of every other factor, which the two groups share. A null assay, target or control type means that the claim is na or unknown. A null level means that the factor does not cover those samples.

docs.title: When the format changes
docs.text:
There is one format at a time. format is a whole number, and the check accepts only the current one. A file with another number is rejected, and the message names the number the check expected.

A change to the format raises the number and rewrites every existing file in the same change. No file stays behind in an older format, and git history is the only record of the old form.

docs.title: Knowledge base
docs.text:
The knowledge base is how seqforge knows what a sequencing library is. It holds one entry per technology: the read layout, the barcode positions, the barcode lists. seqforge scores your files against every entry to find the one the bytes match. The entry it picks decides how your data is parsed.

You don't choose an entry; the bytes do. These pages are here so you can see what seqforge recognises, and understand the answer when it tells you what your data is.

docs.title: Supported assays
docs.text: assay what it is told apart by 10x Chromium 3' v3 / v3.1 droplet single-cell, current 3' kit 28 bp barcode read + 10x's barcode list 10x Chromium 3' v2 droplet single-cell, previous 3' kit 26 bp barcode read (2 bp shorter than v3) BD Rhapsody WTA microwell single-cell, 3-block cell label two fixed linkers + three barcode lists SPLiT-seq instrument-free split-pool single-cell two fixed linkers + three round-barcode lists Bulk RNA-seq plain bulk RNA-seq, no barcodes; paired-end or single-end the absence of a barcode read

docs.title: How the entries are organized
docs.text:
Related chemistries are grouped into a family. The 10x 3' family, for example, is one loose pattern: "a 16 bp barcode in a 26–28 bp read". It first says "this is 10x 3' something". Then it descends to the exact member (v2, v3, or v3.1) by read length and barcode list. So seqforge can recognise a family from a vague metadata mention and still pin the exact chemistry from the bytes.

Some chemistries look the same in the reads and are processed the same way, such as v3 and v3.1. These are recorded under both names, and no question is asked. Two that look alike but are processed differently are told apart by whatever can, usually the barcode list. If nothing can, seqforge asks you rather than guessing.

docs.title: Adding a technology
docs.text:
Every entry is executable: it declares a chemistry precisely enough that seqforge can generate synthetic reads from it, probe them, and check it recovers what it declared. If you want to teach seqforge a new chemistry, the Adding a technology tutorial walks through it.

For the human-readable descriptions of each library structure, the Teichmann Lab's scg_lib_structs is an excellent reference, and each assay page below links to its entry there where one exists.

docs.title: 10x Chromium Single Cell 3' Gene Expression v2
docs.text: Droplet single-cell RNA-seq — the generation before v3. Every droplet holds one gel bead, which tags all of a cell's transcripts with the same cell barcode and each individual mRNA molecule with a unique UMI. That lets you count molecules per gene per cell.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
Two reads come off the sequencer:

read length what it holds R1 26 bp a 16 bp cell barcode + a 10 bp UMI R2 open-ended the cDNA (the transcript itself), read sense to the mRNA

The cell barcode is drawn from 10x's published 737K-august-2016 list (~737,000 barcodes).

docs.title: How seqforge tells v2 apart from v3
docs.text:
The only difference visible in the reads is R1 length: v2 is 16 + 10 = 26 bp; v3 is 16 + 12 = 28 bp. That 2 bp gap is decisive on its own, so seqforge separates v2 from v3 by read geometry alone — before it ever consults a barcode list. The two are never confused. (Their whitelists differ too — 737K-august-2016 vs 3M-february-2018 — but length settles it first.)

If a paper or database says "v2" while the reads are actually 28 bp, seqforge does not quietly pick one. It surfaces the disagreement (metadata says 26 bp, the bytes say 28 bp) and hands it to a human — the bytes decide what the data is.

docs.title: The one neighbour the reads cannot decide
docs.text:
5' v1/v2 is this entry's twin in every byte. It has the same 26 bp R1 (16 bp barcode + 10 bp UMI), the same open-ended cDNA R2, and — the part that closes every cheap route — the same 737K-august-2016 whitelist. Both entries point at the same file, so the barcode list cannot break the tie either. The backends differ in exactly one parameter, soloStrand, and no probe can observe it: 5' reads the transcript from the other end.

That makes it the only read-undecidable pair in this knowledge base, and worth knowing because the resolver's behaviour changes here. Rather than pick, it reaches for metadata (papers say "5'" or "3'" reliably even when they are vague about the version) or a trial alignment, and asks a human if neither answers. Before the 5' entry existed a 5' library resolved silently to this spec and compiled soloStrand Forward — a measured 0.5–0.6 gene-expression correlation against >0.98 for the right orientation, at exit 0, with nothing red.

None of this is true of v3: at 28 bp its geometry-mates each carry their own list, so the barcode list settles them.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• The barcode read can go missing on SRA. fasterq-dump without --include-technical drops R1 entirely; seqforge blocks rather than guessing which file is which. Re-fetch with --include-technical, or pull the submitter's original files.
  • SRA rewrites read-name headers, so seqforge never trusts them when grouping files into samples.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Read structure cross-checked against scg_lib_structs — 10x Chromium 3' (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY), which lays out the v2–v4 kits side by side. The exact, machine-readable definition seqforge uses lives in this entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: 10x Chromium Single Cell 3' Gene Expression v3 (and v3.1)
docs.text:
Droplet single-cell RNA-seq — the current-generation 3' kit. Every droplet holds one gel bead, which tags all of a cell's transcripts with the same cell barcode and each mRNA molecule with a unique UMI.

This page covers both v3 and v3.1. To a sequencer they are the same library, and seqforge processes them identically — see v3 vs v3.1 below.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
read length what it holds R1 28 bp a 16 bp cell barcode + a 12 bp UMI R2 open-ended the cDNA (the transcript itself), read sense to the mRNA

The cell barcode is drawn from 10x's 3M-february-2018 list (~6.8 million barcodes). Index reads (I1/I2) may or may not be present; seqforge doesn't need them.

Names you'll see in the wild: "10x 3' v3", "Chromium 3' v3", "SC3Pv3", "single cell 3-prime v3", "Next GEM 3' v3.1". Papers often write only "10x 3' v3" for a v3.1 run, or name the kit and not the version — which changes nothing, as the next section explains.

docs.title: v3 vs v3.1
docs.text: They are identical to seqforge: same read layout, same barcode list, same alignment settings. No probe can tell them apart from the reads, and none needs to — so seqforge records both names and asks you nothing. v3.1 exists as its own knowledge-base entry only so that "these two really are identical" is something the test suite re-checks on every build, rather than a claim sitting in a comment.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart from other chemistries
docs.text:
• v2 — a 16 bp barcode + a 10 bp UMI makes a 26 bp R1 (vs v3's 28 bp), on a different list. The 2 bp length difference alone separates them.
  • Multiome (ARC), GEM-X 3' v4 and 5' v3 all produce the same 28 bp / 16+12 layout. Four chemistries, one geometry, told apart pairwise by which of four barcode lists hits — each carries its own. Geometry narrows to the cohort; the list picks the member. 5' v3 does read the cDNA in the opposite direction, but no probe can see that; its own 3M-5pgex-jan-2023 list is what actually settles it.
  • The 5' kit geometry genuinely cannot reach is one generation back. 5' v1/v2 is a 26 bp read drawn from 3' v2's whitelist, so that pair shares layout and list alike and is the only read-undecidable one in this knowledge base — settled by metadata or a trial alignment, never by bytes. It is a claim about a version pairing, not about "5'", and it does not apply here.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• The barcode read can go missing on SRA. fasterq-dump without --include-technical drops the 28 bp R1; seqforge blocks rather than inventing a barcode read from a filename. Re-fetch with --include-technical, or pull the submitter's original files.
  • A pre-trimmed upload (R1 no longer a single fixed length) shifts the barcode offsets — seqforge refuses rather than reading the barcode from the wrong place.
  • SRA rewrites read-name headers, so seqforge never trusts them when grouping files into samples.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Read structure cross-checked against scg_lib_structs — 10x Chromium 3' (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY). The exact, machine-readable definition seqforge uses lives in each entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: BD Rhapsody WTA (Whole Transcriptome Analysis)
docs.text:
BD Biosciences' droplet-free single-cell 3' RNA-seq. Cells are captured in a microwell plate and tagged with a cell label built from three barcode blocks on the capture bead, plus a UMI on each molecule.

BD ships this chemistry in two bead generations, and seqforge recognizes and compiles both automatically, from the reads. The original fixed-position bead is described first; the 2022 Enhanced bead — with its variable-length diversity insert — is described below. seqforge tells the two apart from the bytes (their linker structure differs), so you never have to declare which bead a dataset used.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
Two reads:

  • R2 = the cDNA (the transcript), read sense to the mRNA.
  • R1 = the bead read: three 9 bp cell-label blocks separated by two fixed linker sequences, then an 8 bp UMI.
segment on R1 length position cell label 1 9 bp 0–9 linker 1 (ACTGGCCTGCGA) 12 bp 9–21 cell label 2 9 bp 21–30 linker 2 (GGTAGCGGTGACA) 13 bp 30–43 cell label 3 9 bp 43–52 UMI 8 bp 52–60

Each cell-label block is drawn from its own published list of 97 9-mers, so there are 97³ ≈ 913,000 possible cell labels. R1 is often sequenced past position 60 into poly(T)/cDNA; those extra bases are ignored.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart
docs.text: The two fixed linker sequences at known positions are the signature — no other supported chemistry has them. Each cell-label block also matches its own barcode list, which both confirms the call and separates BD Rhapsody from a plain bulk paired-end library (bulk has no barcode list to match).

docs.title: Strand
docs.text: The bead's capture oligo ends in poly(dT), which primes off the mRNA poly(A) tail, so R2 reads the cDNA sense to the transcript — a standard 3' poly-dT library, like 10x 3'. Getting this backwards would leave most reads uncounted while the aligner still exits cleanly, so seqforge derives it from the bead chemistry rather than guessing.

docs.title: Enhanced beads (2022)
docs.text:
In 2022 BD introduced Enhanced Cell Capture Beads, the current chemistry. The cell labels work the same way — three 9 bp blocks read off the bead — but two things change:

  • A short diversity insert of 0–3 bp (one of nothing, A, GT, or TCA) is added at the very start of Read 1, to stagger the reads and cut the amount of PhiX needed.
  • The two linkers shrink to GTGA and GACA (4 bp each), from v1's 12 and 13 bp.

So Enhanced Read 1 reads:

[0–3 bp insert] [CLS1 · 9] GTGA [CLS2 · 9] GACA [CLS3 · 9] [UMI · 8]

There are two sub-versions, differing only in the cell-label lists: 96 or 384 sequences per block (the 384-list "Enhanced v2" allows more cell labels). The read layout is otherwise identical.

docs.title: How seqforge handles the Enhanced bead
docs.text:
seqforge recognizes and compiles the Enhanced bead automatically — you do not tell it the bead generation, and you do not pre-trim the diversity insert.

  • Recognition. The diversity insert shifts every barcode by a different amount from one read to the next, so the positions are not fixed. seqforge finds the GTGA…GACA linker frame in each read (tolerating the 0–3 bp stagger and sequencing error), then reads the cell-label and UMI blocks relative to it. The presence of that frame is what separates Enhanced from the original bead, whose longer ACTGGCCTGCGA/GGTAGCGGTGACA linkers sit at fixed positions instead.
  • 96 vs 384. The two Enhanced sub-versions have identical read layout and differ only in which cell-label list their blocks match, so seqforge picks the one the barcodes actually hit — exactly how it tells 10x v2 from v3. The 96-plex bead reuses the original bead's cell-label lists; the 384-plex lists ship with seqforge too.
  • Compilation. seqforge maps Enhanced reads with STARsolo's adapter anchor — no pre-trimming — and derives the exact settings STAR's author endorsed in issue #1607 straight from the read layout:
STAR --soloType CB_UMI_Complex \
     --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA \
     --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 \
     --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 \
     --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1.txt BD_CLS2.txt BD_CLS3.txt

The adapter NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA is CLS1(9) + GTGA + CLS2(9) + GACA; STARsolo finds it in each read and reads the barcodes relative to it, so the variable insert at the front takes care of itself. For a reproducible reference workflow spanning every bead generation, see rhapsodist.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Read structure, linker sequences, and barcode lists pinned from scg_lib_structs — BD Rhapsody (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY), cross-checked against the seqspec bd_rhapsody_v1 example and the STARsolo maintainer's endorsed settings. The exact, machine-readable definition seqforge uses lives in this entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: Bulk Illumina RNA-seq
docs.text: Standard bulk RNA-seq on an Illumina sequencer: cDNA reads with no cell barcode and no UMI. Every base is transcript sequence — there's nothing to demultiplex into cells. seqforge aligns these with plain STAR and counts genes, rather than STARsolo.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
• R1 and R2 are the two ends of the same cDNA fragment (a mate pair). Both are transcript sequence, typically 75–150 bp.
  • No barcode, no UMI, no whitelist.

Paired-end and single-end are one entry, not two. They are the same chemistry run two ways, so this entry declares the paired layout and names R1 alone as its single-end configuration; the bytes choose between them, and a deposit of one file is explained rather than refused. Nothing about the reads is written down twice, so the two configurations cannot drift apart.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart from single-cell
docs.text:
It's the absence of a barcode that identifies bulk. seqforge looks for a short, low-diversity technical read — the tell-tale of a cell barcode — and finds none, just two long, near-unique cDNA mates. A single-cell barcode read is short (26–28 bp) and repeats the same 16 bp prefix across reads; a bulk mate is long and near-unique from the first base, so a barcode read can never be mistaken for bulk cDNA.

Because this entry demands so little, it also serves as the fallback for any paired-end data. That's deliberate: when a real single-cell library (BD Rhapsody, SPLiT-seq) happens to share this loose shape, seqforge falls back to the barcode-list check to make sure it never quietly treats a single-cell library as bulk.

docs.title: Coverage note
docs.text: This is the poly-A branch. Explicit strand-protocol handling isn't modeled yet.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The exact, machine-readable definition seqforge uses lives in this entry's spec.yaml. (scg_lib_structs documents single-cell library structures; plain bulk RNA-seq isn't one of them, so there's no page to link.)

docs.title: SPLiT-seq (split-pool combinatorial barcoding)
docs.text:
A single-cell RNA-seq method that needs no special instrument. Instead of one droplet per cell, cells are barcoded by splitting and pooling them through several rounds of labeling. After three rounds, each cell carries a unique combination of three barcodes.

This entry covers the original published SPLiT-seq (Rosenberg et al., Science 2018). Parse Biosciences' Evercode is a separate commercial descendant with different linkers and barcodes — a different chemistry, not covered here.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
• Read 1 = the cDNA (the transcript).
  • Read 2 = the barcode read: a 10 bp UMI, then three 8 bp round-barcodes separated by two fixed 30 bp linkers.
[10 bp UMI] [8 bp round-3] --linker1-- [8 bp round-2] --linker2-- [8 bp round-1]

A cell's identity is the combination of its round-1, round-2, and round-3 barcodes; each round draws from a list of ~96 barcodes.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart
docs.text: Like BD Rhapsody, the two fixed linker sequences at known positions are the signature, and each round-barcode matches its own list. The exact linker lengths matter: the original 2018 chemistry puts round-1 at a different position than the later Parse chemistry, so a position copied from the wrong source silently mismatches. seqforge pins the original layout from the paper's own oligos.

docs.title: Status: one question still open
docs.text:
SPLiT-seq is the pilot's generalization test. It exercises machinery the 10x entries don't: 8 bp barcodes instead of 16, and a barcode split combinatorially across a read. All three round-barcode lists ship packed with seqforge, so the entry resolves and compiles from bytes alone. One thing is still unconfirmed:

  • The strand has not been checked against real data. It's derived from the paper's oligos and backed by the authors' own pipeline. Both point the same way, and no source claims the opposite. But most pipelines never chose the strand; they inherited a default. So agreement with them is weaker evidence than it looks. The decisive check is to run the paper's own data both ways. The correct strand assigns roughly ten times more reads.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Read structure and linker sequences pinned from scg_lib_structs — SPLiT-seq (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY) and independently reconstructed from the paper's oligo tables (Rosenberg et al., Science 2018). The exact, machine-readable definition seqforge uses lives in this entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: Adding a technology
docs.text:
The knowledge base has one directory per sequencing technology. Adding one is how seqforge learns to recognise something new. The rule that makes it trustworthy: every entry is executable and self-testing. You describe the technology, and the tests come from the description.

kb/specs/<technology>/
    spec.yaml     what the machine needs: read layout, barcode positions, how to detect it
    README.md     what a human needs: how the assay works, what it gets confused with, gotchas

docs.title: The round-trip is the whole idea
docs.text:
spec.yaml describes the reads well enough to generate reads. So generate them, probe them, and check you get back what you declared:

flowchart LR
    S["<span style='color:#fff'>spec.yaml<br/><i>what you declared</i></span>"] --> G["generate<br/>synthetic FASTQ"]
    G --> P["probe<br/><i>the real code path</i>"]
    P --> REC["<span style='color:#fff'>what was recovered</span>"]
    S -.->|"must match"| REC

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class S,REC artifact
pixi run -- seqforge kb roundtrip <technology>

If what comes out does not match what you declared, your entry is wrong — no real data, no download, no waiting. This runs for every entry automatically: the test collects the entries that exist, so adding a directory covers it.

docs.title: Declaring what you get confused with
docs.text:
Some technologies are genuinely indistinguishable from the reads — two versions of 10x share the same geometry and the same barcode list. That is a fact about the chemistry, not a gap in our code, so write it down:

confusable_with:
  - id: some-other-tech
    relationship: processing_equivalent   # or: processing_divergent
    distinguishable_by: [onlist]          # what CAN tell them apart
    note: >
      Why they collide, in a sentence someone can check.
  • processing_equivalent — identical settings, so the distinction cannot change anything. Record both names, ask nothing.
  • processing_divergent — different pipelines. Must be resolved, by whatever distinguishable_by names.

You cannot get away with not declaring it. A check generates each entry's reads and asks every other entry whether it would claim them using only the cheap probes. If it would, and you did not declare it, that is an error.

docs.title: Two things that will trip you up
docs.text:
Only say how to parse, never what to count. backend.params is for what the bytes decide — where the barcode starts, how long it is, which strand. Not for what to count. An allowlist enforces it, because getting it wrong cost a measured 40.7% of a nuclear library: counting rules were filed as a property of the chemistry, when the chemistry is identical for cells and nuclei.

Never type a barcode position from memory. Positions are computed from the element coordinates you declare. SPLiT-seq's first-round barcode sits at 86–93 in the original and 78–85 in the commercial descendant — a remembered number is a coin flip between two real chemistries.

docs.title: Before you open the pull request
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge kb lint <technology>      # schema + the parse/count line
pixi run -- seqforge kb roundtrip <technology> # declared == recovered
pixi run -- seqforge kb show <technology>      # eyeball it
pixi run -- pre-commit install                 # once per clone: format, lint, typecheck
pixi run check                                 # the full suite, where the pairwise checks live

docs.title: Step-by-step: compiling a real dataset
docs.text:
This is the detailed walkthrough — the pipeline one verb at a time. If you just want to compile a dataset, driving seqforge with Claude is the shorter path; come here when you want to see, and inspect, each stage.

This is the worked example, start to finish, on the dataset seqforge was built against: PRJNA1027859 — six single-nucleus RNA-seq runs of adult C. elegans neurons, wild-type versus daf-2 mutants, from Cell Genomics 2024.

You will end with a Snakefile you can submit. seqforge does not submit it — no Slurm profile, no sbatch, no executor. Its output is artifacts, and the last one runs.

Everything below is real output from a real run. Where a command is slow or needs 220 GB of FASTQ, that is said.

docs.title: 0. What you have
docs.text:
Two things, and one of them is optional:

data/
  SRX24283130/SRR28716558_1.fastq.gz    # 12 files, one directory per experiment,
  SRX24283130/SRR28716558_2.fastq.gz    # which is how `fasterq-dump` wrote them
  ...
info/
  paper.pdf                             # optional

Plus an accession, PRJNA1027859, which is also optional — plenty of data never had one. Each of the three inputs makes the answer richer; none of them is required, and none of them is trusted.

docs.title: The short version: one pass
docs.text:
If you just want the manifest and the Snakefile, seqforge run does the whole thing and prints one summary:

pixi run -- seqforge run data/*/*.fastq.gz \
    --accession PRJNA1027859 --doc info/paper.pdf \
    --assembly ce11 --annotation WS298 --fastq-dir data

It chains every stage below — records, the paper, the manifest, the recipe, the Snakefile — stops at the first refusal, and writes everything under seqforge/. The genome is the one argument with no default (a wrong one aligns cleanly and exits 0, so it will not guess). Reading the paper uses a language model through the lab's model gateway: open a tunnel to it and set LABLLM_GATEWAY to its local address (Reach the lab gateway). It spends at most a dollar unless --ceiling-usd says otherwise. Add --no-llm to skip prose and stay fully deterministic.

The rest of this page walks the same pipeline one verb at a time — which is what you want when a step needs inspecting, and what run is doing for you when it does not.

docs.title: 1. Ask the bytes what this is
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge resolve score data/SRX24283130/*.fastq.gz

This reads the first 2 000 reads of each file and never more (it is bounded by --max-reads and by a 256 MB decompressed cap; a code path that could stream a whole multi-GB FASTQ is a bug here, not a slow path). Two thousand reads is plenty — the chemistry is the same whether you look at one thousand or two hundred thousand — and you can raise --max-reads to sample more of a full-size file. It scores every technology in the knowledge base against what it saw and prints the ranked candidates, the role assigned to each file, and the rung that settled it.

Note what it does not do: read the filenames for meaning. _1 and _2 are fasterq-dump's dump order and say nothing about which read is the barcode. Roles come from bytes.

Add --explain to see the evidence matrix — one row per read role, one column per file — when you want to know why.

docs.title: 2. Ask the archive what it declares
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge io records PRJNA1027859

{
  "records": "seqforge/records/PRJNA1027859.json",
  "query": "PRJNA1027859",
  "source": "ncbi-sra+biosample",
  "n": { "project": 1, "sample": 6, "experiment": 6, "run": 6 }
}

Four levels, joined by the archive's own accessions:

BioProject PRJNA1027859      title, abstract, centre, data type
  └─ BioSample SAMN40935621     strain=CQ758, tissue=Neurons, sex=hermaphrodite, dev_stage=Adult Day 1
       └─ Experiment SRX24283135   instrument, library strategy, and the protocol paragraph
            └─ Run SRR28716553        the alias "Rep3 daf2 reads", and your files

This verb is a transcriber. It reports what the submitter typed and stops; it decides nothing.

The run and sample records are what match each of your files to its sample, and the records declare the organism and the project. What each sample was (its strain, tissue or treatment) is not part of the compiled manifest: a study reading holds those (see Study workflow).

docs.title: 3. Write down what the data IS
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge manifest fill data/*/*.fastq.gz --accession PRJNA1027859

Two resolvers run here, and they answer different questions.

resolve score reads the bytes and decides the library: which chemistry, which file is which read. The metadata resolver reads the records and decides which sample each file is. Neither is shown the other's input — the metadata resolver is handed file names and hashes, not the probe's output, because the join is made by the names the records declare.

Both can refuse.

You get seqforge/manifest.yaml:

experiment:
  organism:
    value: 6239
    basis: asserted
    evidence: [SAMN40935616, SAMN40935617, SAMN40935618,
               SAMN40935619, SAMN40935620, SAMN40935621]
    confidence: null
    rung: 0
  project:
    accession: PRJNA1027859
    title: A Single-Nucleus Atlas of Adult C. elegans Neurons Reveals GPCR and Insulin-signaling Profiles
    center: Princeton University
    data_type: raw sequence reads
  samples:
    - sample_id: SAMN40935616
      accession: SAMN40935616
      file_uris: [SRX24283130/SRR28716558_1.fastq.gz, SRX24283130/SRR28716558_2.fastq.gz]
    # ... five more

Two things worth reading closely.

You did not pass --organism. The record declares it, and the manifest cites the six BioSamples it came from. A flag still wins if you pass one — a human typing a taxid is asserting it now, having looked — but nothing is defaulted. There is no default taxid and there must not be: a wrong one aligns cleanly against the wrong genome, exits 0, and nothing downstream ever asks again.

confidence: null is the informative value. It means nothing was judged. Copying the taxid out of a BioSample record is a transcription — basis: asserted plus the record accessions in evidence already says everything true about how we know it. A 1.0 there would invite the question it cannot answer ("you are certain it is 6239?"). We are certain the records declare it, which is a different claim and the one we make.

docs.title: If you have no accession
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge manifest fill reads/*.fastq.gz --organism 6239

That works, and it is the common case. Files are grouped into runs by name, and each run becomes a sample. Exit 0, and a manifest that is just as true.

docs.title: If the accession does not match your files
docs.text:
That is a refusal, not a shrug:

RECORD_JOIN_INCOMPLETE: PRJNA1027859 declares 6 run(s) (SRR28716553, ...), and 1 file(s) on disk
match none of them by run accession or by the original filenames the record declares: mystery_1.fastq.gz

Half-joining would leave that file with no sample while the manifest still read as though it described everything.

docs.title: 4. Let the model read the prose (optional)
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge harvest extract info/paper.pdf --records seqforge/records/PRJNA1027859.json
pixi run -- seqforge manifest fill data/*/*.fastq.gz --accession PRJNA1027859 \
    --assertions seqforge/logs/assertions.json

This is the only stage that touches a language model. A model writes an answer only where code can check it. Here that means two jobs: turn prose into claims that carry a quote, and settle an ambiguity code has already flagged. Code decides whether each answer stands. Everything else in seqforge is a verifier.

Every claim it returns carries a verbatim quote. Code — not the model — greps that quote back into the normalized document, computes the offsets, and checks that the quote actually supports the value. A claim that fails either check is discarded.

What the model is asked. From a paper: the chemistry, whether the input was cells or nuclei, the organism and the accessions. --records renders each experiment record as its own document, and its protocol paragraph is asked for the chemistry and nothing else. Sample and run records, and the study abstract, are asked nothing. What each sample was is not the compiler's question; a study reading answers it.

A chemistry claim is a hint, never evidence. It can break a tie the bytes cannot settle, and a disagreement between what the paper claims and what the bytes show is a question for you, never something code picks.

docs.title: 5. Write down what you want DONE with it
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge processing new seqforge/manifest.yaml \
    --assembly ce11 --annotation WS298 --out seqforge/processing.yaml

A dataset is immutable; what you do with it is a choice. So they are two files, and there are as many processing manifests as you care to run. If you find yourself editing manifest.yaml to change how something is processed, stop — that is the bug the split exists to prevent.

manifest fill takes no genome, deliberately. Choosing a reference is intent, not something you learn by probing bytes.

You will not need --quantify here. The default counts all five STARsolo features in one pass — one alignment, five counting rules — so this being single-nucleus data (full of unspliced pre-mRNA, and therefore needing GeneFull) costs you no decision and no question. Where every answer is affordable, produce every answer.

docs.title: 6. Compile
docs.text:
pixi run -- seqforge compose seqforge/manifest.yaml \
    --processing seqforge/processing.yaml --fastq-dir data

{
  "snakefile_path": "seqforge/pipeline/default-d94c737eb677/Snakefile",
  "config_path": "seqforge/pipeline/default-d94c737eb677/config.yaml",
  "units_path": "seqforge/pipeline/default-d94c737eb677/units.tsv",
  "gate": {
    "params": { "status": "pass", "reason": [] },
    "wiring": { "status": "pass", "reason": [] },
    "e2e": { "status": "skip", "reason": ["the end-to-end toolchain is incomplete here: ['STAR'] absent"] }
  }
}

The directory is named for the recipe plus the first 12 characters of the run id. The run id is H(dataset ⊕ processing ⊕ kb ⊕ workflow), so compiling this dataset a second way gives you a second directory rather than silently overwriting the first — and the dataset's own hash does not move.

That hash is one run's, and it will not be yours. workflow in the expression is the compiler's own version, so a release moves the directory name for the same dataset and the same recipe. Step 7 therefore takes the path from your own output, never from this page.

Each gate carries its own reason beside its verdict, because a verdict alone does not say what to do: a failing wiring gate hands back what snakemake said, and a skip says what it was waiting for.

The gates:

  • params — the semantic checks a dry run cannot make. Is --soloUMIlen 12 when the reads carry a 12 bp UMI? Does --readFilesIn put the cDNA read where the cDNA read belongs? These are the bugs a config compiler actually produces, and they fail silently: STARsolo exits 0 and emits a matrix that merely looks like a thin dataset.
  • wiring — snakemake -n over a throwaway replica. It proves the workflow plans jobs. A dry run that plans nothing also exits 0, so the gate looks rather than trusting the code.
  • e2e — the real count-matrix run. Reported skip, never silently pass: it needs STAR and a genome, and a gate that says "pass" because it never ran would let green CI be mistaken for coverage.

docs.title: 7. Submit it
docs.text:
The directory to go into is the one compose just printed — its snakefile_path, minus the Snakefile on the end:

cd seqforge/pipeline/<the-directory-compose-named>
snakemake --software-deployment-method apptainer

This part is yours. seqforge has no opinion about your scheduler, and it will not grow one.

--software-deployment-method apptainer is what makes the alignment rule run inside the pinned liulab-runtime image. Without it snakemake ignores the container: directive entirely and STAR comes from your PATH: the run still works, and it is no longer pinned.

Run it on one machine. The pipeline loads the genome index into shared memory once and every mapping job attaches to that one copy, so several samples mapping at the same time cost one index between them rather than one apiece — on a human genome that is the difference between ~31 GB and ~31 GB times however many jobs are running. Spreading the jobs across machines with a cluster profile still satisfies every dependency in the workflow and silently gives each job its own copy, because an edge guarantees order, never that two jobs share a machine. Scale comes from running many pipelines at once, not from fanning one out. Give the run a whole machine and let --cores decide how many samples map at a time.

The default target is all, which demands the matrices — one <sample>.h5ad per sample, plus a <sample>.velocyto.h5ad — not a folder that might be empty.

The 111 MB barcode whitelist is not in that directory, and should not be. A rule builds it, STAR reads it once, and snakemake deletes it.

docs.title: When the project isn't uniform
docs.text: Every run of this dataset is the same 10x chemistry, so it compiled to one manifest and one Snakefile. A study that mixes chemistries — 10x v2 and v3 libraries in one series, say — compiles to one of each per assay: seqforge/<assay>/manifest.yaml and its own Snakefile, one per chemistry, with the split decided from the bytes rather than by you. Two project-level files then sit at the top, sample_metadata.tsv (every sample across every assay, one row each) and project.yaml (the assay index), and you submit each assay's Snakefile. The uniform case here is just the single-assay degenerate one — same artifacts, no subdirectory. See the two artifacts for why a project splits this way.

docs.title: Compiling a dataset with Claude
docs.text:
The easiest way to use seqforge is to not run it yourself. You describe your data to Claude Code in plain words, and Claude drives seqforge for you — figuring out the technology, which file is which read, and how to compile it into a pipeline you can run.

You don't need to know what chemistry your data is, which file holds the barcodes, or what any of the flags mean. That is exactly the knowledge seqforge exists to recover from the files themselves. Your job is to point at the data and say what you want.

This page is the short, friendly path. When you want to see every step and inspect it, the step-by-step tutorial walks the same pipeline one command at a time.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Install seqforge — see Getting started. One pixi install.

  2. Install the Claude skills. seqforge ships a set of skills that teach Claude how to drive it safely. Install them once:

    pixi run install-skills

  3. Reach the model gateway for reading prose. One stage — reading a paper or a sample sheet — uses a language model, through the lab's model gateway. Open a tunnel to it and set LABLLM_GATEWAY to its local address (Reach the lab gateway); you need no provider key. If you have no paper to read, you can skip this and stay fully offline.

That's it. From here on you just talk to Claude.

docs.title: Compile a dataset
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in the folder with your data and describe what you have. A good request names three things: where the files are, any extra context (an accession, a paper, a sample sheet), and the genome to align against.

Compile the single-cell RNA-seq data in ./data with seqforge. It's accession PRJNA1027859, and the paper is ./info/paper.pdf. Align against the ce11 genome, annotation WS298.

Claude takes it from there. Behind the scenes it runs the seqforge compiler — reading the bytes, pulling what the archive declares, mining the paper for anything useful — and hands you back two things: a manifest (what your data actually is) and a Snakefile (the pipeline that processes it). A minute or two, paper included.

You don't have to give it all three inputs. The files alone are enough:

Compile the FASTQ files in ./reads with seqforge, against the hg38 genome with the GENCODE annotation.

The accession and the paper each make the answer richer — the archive's own sample for each file, the organism, a hint about the kit — but plenty of data never had either, and that's a normal, fully supported case.

docs.title: The one thing you have to decide
docs.text: There is exactly one choice seqforge will not make for you: the genome. A wrong genome still aligns cleanly and still produces a count matrix — it's just quietly wrong, and nothing downstream ever notices. So seqforge refuses to guess, and Claude will ask you for it if you didn't say. Everything else — the technology, which read is the barcode, how long the barcodes are, which strand — is read from the files and never guessed.

docs.title: When Claude stops and asks
docs.text:
seqforge is built to refuse rather than guess. If something is genuinely ambiguous, or the files don't match the accession you gave, Claude will stop and tell you exactly what's wrong — it won't paper over it with a plausible-looking answer. That pause is the tool working. A refusal is cheap; a confidently wrong count matrix is not, because you may not find out for months.

So if Claude comes back with a question instead of a Snakefile, read it — it's naming a real decision only you can make.

docs.title: Run it in a script (headless)
docs.text:
The same thing works without opening an interactive session, which is how you'd batch many datasets:

claude -p "Compile the data in $(pwd)/data with seqforge. Accession PRJNA1027859, paper in
info/paper.pdf, align against ce11 / WS298. Use this directory as the workspace."

Point it at each dataset in a loop and you have a headless pipeline that turns a folder of FASTQ files into a runnable Snakefile, one dataset at a time.

docs.title: What you get: a look inside seqforge/
docs.text:
Everything Claude produces lands in a seqforge/ folder next to your data. The top level holds the things you actually reach for; the rest is tidied into named subfolders:

seqforge/
  manifest.yaml         what your data IS — the technology, the samples, their metadata
  processing.yaml       what to DO with it — the genome and the flags
  project.yaml          a one-glance index of the whole project
  sample_metadata.tsv   every sample, one row each

  pipeline/             the Snakefile you submit, and its config
  records/              what the archive declared, and any papers you handed in
  logs/                 what the paper-reading cost, and the claims it found
  cache/                working files, safe to delete

Two files are the heart of it. manifest.yaml is what your data is — settled once, never rewritten. processing.yaml is what to do with it — the genome, the recipe — and you can have several. Want to align the same data to a different genome? That's a new processing.yaml, never an edit to the manifest. (Why they're split, and why it matters, is in the two artifacts.)

The thing you submit lives under pipeline/: a Snakefile, ready to run. seqforge stops there on purpose — it does not submit jobs, has no opinion about your scheduler, and won't grow one. The last artifact is a file you run:

cd seqforge/pipeline/<the-directory-Claude-made>
snakemake --software-deployment-method apptainer

That produces one .h5ad count matrix per sample. The step-by-step tutorial explains that command, including why the --software-deployment-method apptainer flag matters and why a pipeline runs on one machine.
